title: Light plane clips car near airport, injuring two people
text:
A light plane has clipped a car while landing near Lilydale Airport, in Melbourne's outer east.

Two people, a woman in her 60s and a man in his 70s, have been taken to hospital in a stable condition with head injuries.

Paramedics assessed another two people at the scene, who did not need emergency care or transport.

Emergency services were called to an incident on MacIntyre Lane in Yering about 2.30pm.

"Crews arrived to find a plane that had come in to land had clipped a car," a Country Fire Authority spokesperson said.

ABC 774 listener Steve told host Charlie Pickering both the light plane and the car appeared damaged.

"It appears that a light plane has come in for a landing, crossing MacIntyre Lane, and has hit the roof of a car," Steve said.

Paramedics assessed four people at the scene. (ABC News)

"The actual plane looks like it's spun around and landed on the runway."

Steve said the driver of the car appeared to have been in shock, with blood on his face.

"It looks as though it hit the windscreen. The windscreen's cracked, and the roof's been dented in," he said.

"It would have been a pretty scary time for the driver and the pilot."

ABC understands the aircraft belongs to the Lilydale Flying School.

The school's website states prior permission from the flying school is required to land.

The flying school has been approached for comment.

MacIntyre Lane was closed past Lilydale Airport, with diversions in place, as emergency services responded.

"There's a massive pile-up of cars there," Steve told ABC 774.

title: Who is Jensen Huang and why is the Nvidia CEO scandal important?
text:
In terms of corporate fallout, what's happened at Nvidia has been huge.

The company, seen as the darling of the AI era, has lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value since it was revealed that its chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Nvidia and Mr Huang are now being sued, accused of ⁠defrauding shareholders by concealing the affair.

Nvidia has both benefited from and brought about the global AI revolution.

And, as CEOs go, few are as synonymous with a company as Jensen Huang.

Jensen Huang has admitted to the company's staff that he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. (Reuters: Steve Marcus, file)

"Treating this simply as a sex scandal misses the point," technology strategist Josh Kennedy-White says.

"The real issue is whether personal access to one of the world's most strategically important executives became a channel for intelligence gathering or influence."

So how did we get here?

Who is Jensen Huang?

Born in Taiwan, Mr Huang moved to the US at the age of nine and at some point, he naturalised as a US citizen.

At 17, he attended university in Oregon where he met his wife Lori Mills, who was two years his senior.

Both were studying electrical engineering and Mr Huang has previously recounted using the pick-up line: "Do you wanna see my homework?"

Jensen Huang said his wife, Lori, supported him unconditionally. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

They had weekly study dates, became lab partners and, five years later, married.

In an interview with a magazine at his alma mater in 2013, he described how his wife's support has always been unconditional.

Jensen Huang and his wife dine with Apple's Tim Cook, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

"Ever since I was 18, she was there believing in me and knowing I could do it. Even when I had self doubts, she didn't," he said.

The two went on to have two children, Spencer and Madison Huang, who both now hold executive roles at Nvidia.

Nvidia's beginnings

In 1993, at a diner in San Jose, Mr Huang met with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, fellow engineers he'd worked with in the chip industry since the late 1980s.

There they came up with Nvidia, starting with just $40,000 in capital. In order to incorporate the business, the three founders chucked in $200 a piece.

Originally gaming was the focus. The founders believed the PC gaming market was set to grow and would need more powerful graphics processing.

The motherboard of a Surface Laptop Ultra containing Nvidia's new RTX Spark chip. (Reuters: Manuel Orbegozo)

After a near business-ending initial failure, Nvidia invented what's regarded as the world's first Graphics Processing Unit in 1999. The chips could make advanced computer graphics allowing for advanced 3D environments in video games and perform huge numbers of calculations in parallel.

It wasn't long before developers realised their uses could go far beyond gaming.

"We created the world's first programmable accelerator," Mr Huang said in 2023.

"And the benefit of an accelerator is whatever you designed it to do, it does it incredibly efficiently."

AI era begins

And so, the era of modern AI was born.

Nvidia's chips, by all accounts, are unparalleled. They're so hot, companies struggle to get their hands on them, and the metrics of Nvidia's growth are dizzying.

To give you a sense of some of the numbers: Its shares have increased some 477,000 per cent since listing in 1999; almost five-fold in the past five years.

Dell Technologies CEO Michael Dell, AMD CEO Lisa Su, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stand together during the "A New Golden Age" summit at the US Institute of Peace. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

For Mr Huang, who is estimated to own about 3.5 per cent of the company, his wealth has skyrocketed.

According to Forbes, he was worth $2 billion in 2017 — and now, about $154 billion, putting him in the top 10 most wealthy people in the world.

Loading...

With his trademark leather jackets and high-profile product launches, Mr Huang is omnipresent at Nvidia.

Its website lists him as co-founder, president, chief executive officer and a member of the board of directors.

"He is Nvidia. [He] clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction, and pulls most of the company's strings himself," Stacy Rasgon, a Bernstein analyst said.

And many of the company's executives are relatives of Huang.

US-China chip war and the Trump factor

Nvidia, and Mr Huang, have walked a fine line balancing the demands of Washington and Beijing.

Nvidia is headquartered in California with the vast majority of its chips produced by the chipmaker TSMC in Taiwan, along with some production in the US and South Korea.

The US restricted the exports of chips to China in 2022, citing it as an issue of national defence.

It's been a huge point of contention between the world's two superpowers with Beijing racing to develop its own semiconductor industry.

Jensen Haung joined a delegation of US tech CEOs and government officials on Donald Trump's state visit to China. (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov)

Mr Huang, who is one of US President Donald Trump's closest allies in Silicon Valley, has tried to push the administration to loosen restrictions.

He's argued that American companies should be able to compete globally and that it would prevent China's chip industry developing too powerfully.

He's had some success. Earlier this year Washington gave the greenlight for Nvidia to sell its second-tier chip (the H200) to Chinese companies, so long as they could take a 25 per cent cut.

There have also been reports about Chinese companies illegally getting access to US chip technology through the backdoor.

One company, for example, is a Singapore cloud computing firm Megaspeed which is being investigated by the US over suspicions it's helping get Nvidia AI chips into China.

The alleged spy scandal

A screen grab from CTI video obtained on November 9, 2026 shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang after comparison with a photograph obtained separately, attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (in black) at a restaurant in Taipei. (Reuters: CTI)

The Wall Street Journal reports Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Mr Huang, was previously Megaspeed's boss.

It was in this capacity that she allegedly met Mr Huang at an Nvidia event in California in 2024. It's not known how long the affair lasted nor where Ms Huang is now. She has not responded to journalist requests for comment.

Now the affair is part of an FBI investigation, with Mr Trump saying he "was amazed" by the allegations.

"I know the FBI is looking into it … I think that he'll be in good shape," he said.

US lawmakers say Congress is likely to tighten China's access to US chips as part of the fallout while Nvidia's board has launched an internal investigation.

Spy tactics may reshape AI race Allegations of espionage between China and the US are nothing new. But a target as big as Jensen Huang could change who wins the AI race.

Beijing has denied the allegations.

"The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Josh Kennedy-White, chief commercial officer at strategic communications firm IN2, said the scandal exposes the danger of making one company and one individual so indispensable to the global AI economy.

"The Huang affair is a reminder that the most valuable target may not be a government official," he told ABC News.

" When corporate leaders control technologies of national importance, their personal vulnerabilities can become strategic vulnerabilities. "

Jensen Huang hasn't tweeted or released anything public since he sent staff a letter on Sunday.

"I owe my family and all of you an apology," he wrote.

"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

title: Data centre builder Firmus says diesel generators only for emergencies
text:
AI data centre builder Firmus Technologies has told a parliamentary inquiry it would only use diesel generators at its sites during emergencies.

Firmus has operational AI data centres in Melbourne and Singapore, and is planning more in Tasmania, South Australia, Indonesia and Malaysia.

AI companies rely on energy-intensive data centres to train large language models and process and respond to queries from AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude.

The Firmus Technologies site in St Leonards, Launceston, showing its research and development lab. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Firmus is building an AI data centre in the Launceston suburb of St Leonards, has approval for another at Long Reach in northern Tasmania, and is seeking approval for a third at Wesley Vale in the north-west.

When Firmus gained planning approval for its Long Reach facility, George Town Council imposed a condition that the 276 backup diesel generators could only be used during emergencies, maintenance and testing.

Community concerns had been raised about the environmental and noise impacts of their use.

A render of Firmus Technologies' proposed AI data centre at Long Reach, near George Town. (Supplied)

Firmus appealed the condition, calling it "unreasonable" and stating it would prevent it from using generators during periods of "energy market stress".

Tasmania's Environment Protection Authority has since sought to join the appeal, stating in its submission that it would have assessed the proposal differently had it known the generators would be used "potentially whenever it is commercially convenient for the operator".

Questions at inquiry over diesel generator use

On Tuesday, Firmus faced a parliamentary inquiry into AI data centres in Tasmania and concerns over diesel generator use were raised.

Firmus hasn't revealed who its customers are for Tasmanian data centres. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Independent MP George Razay asked Firmus how often it would use its diesel generators.

"Our intent with regards to diesel generators is they're backup generation," Firmus energy manager Paul Grzinic responded.

Firmus's Paul Grzinic told the inquiry, the company was seeking clarification of the definition of "emergency". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"They are not intended — as others have claimed — for us to run these when commercially convenient, or any other means other than in an emergency situation."

Greens MP and acting inquiry chair Tabatha Badger pressed the issue.

"You say it's only for emergency use — that's what the condition was imposed by the council — and yet you're appealing that," she said.

"So you can understand for Tasmanians listening, that's not going to add up and make a whole lot of sense."

Mr Grzinic said he could not speak in detail about the appeal while it was ongoing.

Tim Rosenfield and Paul Grzinic appearing before the Tasmanian committee. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"We're just seeking, effectively, clarification of — it's quite broad, that definition of emergency — so we're just seeking clarification," he said.

Firmus is setting up a research and development facility at its Wesley Vale site to investigate ways to reduce reliance on backup diesel generators.

Customers not revealed

Asked by Ms Badger who Firmus's customers were, co-chief executive and co-founder Tim Rosenfield declined to say.

"Like any commercial data centre developer, if you look at some of our listed peers in Australia, it's not normal practice to disclose who your customers are at any particular location," he said.

"That can be for security reasons or contractual confidentiality reasons, so I wouldn't expect it to be an expectation for us to do so — it's just not an industry norm.

"And I don't think it's something our customers would be particularly happy with us doing."

Construction underway at Firmus' St Leonards site. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The company has previously said it has contracted the Launceston and Wesley Vale facilities to customers, while Long Reach was under option to a customer.

'No change' to plans despite cancelled float

Last month, Firmus was forced to withdraw its highly-anticipated initial public offering (IPO) — set to be the biggest float in the Australian share market since Telstra in 1997 — after lacklustre interest from investors.

Professor Razay asked about the impact that had on Firmus's plans, but Mr Rosenfield said it did not change anything.

Tim Rosenfield said growth plans for Firmus were still on track, despite the abandoned IPO. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"We have extremely supportive shareholders who are backing us to grow exactly the same way we've always planned to grow," Mr Rosenfield said.

" An IPO is just a means to a transaction, we decided not to pursue that particular transaction but that doesn't change our growth plans — not one bit. "

The inquiry will continue hearings with stakeholders about AI data centres in Tasmania before making recommendations to the government.

title: Larrakia custodians seek heritage listing to stop Lee Point housing project
text:
Two Larrakia custodians have requested an emergency heritage listing by the Commonwealth in an attempt to prevent the federal government from building a large housing estate at Darwin's Lee Point.

Lorraine Williams and Tibby Quall argued in their application to the Australian Heritage Council and the federal environment minister that the site approved for 600 private and 200 defence personnel houses should be protected as the "Binybara cultural heritage landscape" for its Indigenous, biodiversity and historical values.

"Hopefully we'll achieve protection for the entire area so that it's not developed, and is left to be natural bush because the land is culturally significant to us and our culture and history," Ms Williams said.

Lorraine Williams says Lee Point should be protected as a cultural landscape. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

" Our culture and our language is written into our lands; this Binybara land has a lot of stories written into it, and a lot of people want to protect it. "

Ms Williams said the housing estate would interfere with the registered Binybara Larrakia sacred site, a rock reef off Lee Point beach, and a sacred women's site in the development area.

"Because we don't have land rights in Darwin, we don't have native title, we're using all of the different acts that are available to us, and this is why we are having to try to protect Binybara under the heritage legislation that's available to us, and we'll keep on fighting until we get full rights to this land," she said.

Larrakia custodians hope the area will be protected as the Binybara cultural heritage landscape. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

During land clearing of one block of its planned 132-hectare development, the federal government developer Defence Housing Australia uncovered Indigenous cultural artefacts including a grinding stone.

Last week, Defence Housing Australia, which has so far built five houses at the site, announced it had revised its Lee Point plan to address biodiversity and sacred site concerns, but Ms Williams said the revisions did not go far enough.

Emergency application could halt work

The Larrakia custodians' lawyer, Ally McAlpine from Environmental Justice Australia, said the heritage nomination included a request for a provisional emergency listing to try to stop further work while the full application was considered.

"This application isn't just about individual sites or objects; it's considering the whole of the peninsula and the particular cultural significance it has to the Larrakia people, its military history significance and its biodiversity and its ecological significance," she said.

The development at Lee Point has sparked four years of protests by members of the public and Larrakia custodians. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

The custodians have argued Lee Point is worthy of joining the six other Northern Territory places on the 127-place national heritage list, which include Kakadu National Park, the Hermannsburg Historic Precinct and Wave Hill Walk Off Route.

Defence Housing Australia revises Lee Point master plan Defence Housing Australia has revised its plan to build an 800-house precinct in Lee Point in Darwin's northern suburbs.

Nominations for heritage listing are assessed by the Australian Heritage Council, and then referred to the federal environment minister for acceptance or rejection.

The Heritage Council's criteria for acceptance include that the place has "outstanding value to the nation" because of its "uncommon, rare or endangered aspects of Australia's natural or cultural history" or a "strong or special association with a particular community or cultural group for social, cultural or spiritual reasons".

To reach the list threshold, a place must have "outstanding heritage value to the Australian community as a whole".

The Heritage Council also considers whether it is more significant compared to other similar places.

Charles Darwin University scientists have assessed Lee Point's tropical eucalyptus woodland habitat as being one of the few remaining Darwin coastal habitats that are important for the survival of endangered species including the black-footed tree rat and the Gouldian finch.

Gouldian finches inhabit Lee Point's tropical eucalyptus woodland. (Supplied: Kacie Austin)

"I want the government to acknowledge that those animals and plants are actually important to Larrakia people and our culture — they are part of our biocultural knowledge and biocultural heritage," Ms Williams said.

Proponents of the housing estate have argued that some of Lee Point's habitat was previously cleared for World War II defence fortifications, the area already hosts a caravan park, and the housing would not interfere with the Binybara site off the coast.

Emergency national heritage nominations have halted developments in the past, including the listing of Tasmania's Tarkine in 2009, which stopped a commercial tourism road and the 2017 listing of Melbourne's St Kilda area, which forced major changes to a railway.

title: Starc's 'opinion hasn't changed' as he disputes Khawaja sandpaper claims
text:
Australian fast bowler Mitchell Starc has rejected Usman Khawaja's claim the 2018 sandpaper ball-tampering plot was known by all members of the team.

Speaking at Fox Cricket's season launch, Starc became the first current player to respond to the revelations in Khawaja's new book, Sabr.

In the book, released today, Khawaja says the plan to use sandpaper on the ball in the Cape Town Test was common knowledge among the team, and his pleas to have the entire squad take the blame fell on deaf ears.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

David Warner, who, along with Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft, was among the only men punished for the scandal, said today that Khawaja's claims were "100 per cent accurate".

But Starc insisted he did not know a substance was being taken onto the field in Cape Town.

"Obviously there are differing opinions of eight years ago," Starc said.

"We were heavily grilled through the process at the time and since. I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.

"We weren't aware anything was taken on the field to be tampered with. We saw it on the big screen in Cape Town."

In 2021, Starc joined fellow bowlers Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon in releasing a statement disputing any suggestion they had wider knowledge of the ball-tampering plans.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands," the 2021 statement said.

Starc said his stance had not changed since that statement was released but that "clearly there are differing versions from differing people".

Starc also said he knew nothing about Khawaja's claim sandpaper had been used to tamper with the ball in the Test before Cape Town.

Mitchell Starc bowls during the second Test of the 2018 series at St. George's Park. (AP: Michael Sheehan)

Earlier today, Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg said there were no plans to reopen the investigation in light of Khawaja's assertions.

"There are specific details in his book that contradict the versions that have been provided by others," Greenberg said.

"It's important to know that back at that time, players were urged to come forward, and they had the opportunity to do so over these past eight years, and that remains the case.

"We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received.

"That includes what we've seen from Usman, and our position hasn't changed on that.

"We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this. I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that."

Starc said he had not spoken to Khawaja in recent days. He said he had not read the new book and "probably won't read it".

title: More homes proposed for entertainment precinct in 'tall over sprawl' plan
text:
Brisbane's entertainment precinct could see building height limits increased and the development of thousands of new homes as part of the council's "tall over sprawl" strategy.

The Fortitude Valley Sustainable Growth Precinct Plan proposes increasing height limits from 30 to 40 storeys at sites between St Pauls Terrace, Brookes Street, along Ann Street and around Cathedral Place.

On the edge of the precinct, height limits would transition to 30 storeys and lower.

The proposed plan will increase height limits in parts of the valley to 40 storeys. (Supplied: Brisbane City Council)

Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said while entertainment precinct rules and noise protections would be strengthened, the council aimed to protect the nightlife and live music scene.

"We've made sure that any new building takes into account the fact that people will be moving into that kind of precinct that's an entertainment precinct, so buildings will need to be built in a way that protects people from noise impacts, that's part of our strict requirement," he said.

" We think two things can coexist really well in the Valley if it's done well and designed well, and that's what we're focused on. "

Adrian Schrinner says the plan would protect the live music scene while creating more room for homes. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The office of Queensland nightlife economy commissioner John Collins has been contacted for comment.

Brisbane goes sky high in a bid to meet housing demand Brisbane City Council is adopting a "sky high" strategy to deal with a projected surge in population over the next 15 years.

The final plan is expected in 2027, with a period of community consultation from November 13 to December 18.

Fortitude Valley is the latest suburb targeted in the "tall over sprawl" strategy, with suburban centres Indooroopilly, Carindale and Nundah earlier earmarked for height increases.

Limited locations around the Indooroopilly and Carindale shopping centres will see an increase to 25 storeys, while height limits near the Nundah village and train station will increase to 15 storeys.

Those changes will go into effect from December 11.

'Tombstone architecture'

Emeritus Professor Brian Roberts, who is also a Fellow of the Planning Institute of Australia said the "tall over sprawl" strategy is "tombstone architecture".

"Monuments, that are not aesthetically pleasing nor do they ensure the city functions in the most effective way," he said.

"40 storeys in the valley, is far too high, it is not the scale of Brisbane."

Brian Roberts says the council's "tall over sprawl" strategy is an example of "disjointed, incremental development". (Supplied)

Mr Roberts is a global expert in "managing cities", having worked for the World Bank and the United Nations, and is currently writing a report on the "Future of Asian Cities" for the United Nations.

Developers in Brisbane prioritise 'luxury' apartments Almost all the new apartments being built around Brisbane are described as some version of "luxury", despite demand for affordable new builds.

He said what Brisbane is turning into is "not urban living" but "disjointed, incremental development".

"And there is literature that shows once you start building over six to seven floors, there are a lot of psychological requirements that need to be looked at as well," he said.

"As you go higher, there is much higher incidence of loneliness for example and all those things that go against well being, which you get when living in well planned areas with good amenities."

Brisbane Residents United spokeswoman Elizabeth Handley urged the council and government to focus on social housing rather than high-rise apartments.

"No matter which way you stretch it and no matter how many storeys you keep adding on top of them, there is — and particularly with this government — no affordable housing component," Ms Handley said.

Elizabeth Handley says the changes risk the city's unique character. (612 ABC: Kenji Sato)

Ms Handley said the city's character was at risk if similar plans kept moving forward.

"I think it's so important that we have these areas in our city where they are slightly creative and they're a little bit grungy," she said.

title: Greens set sights on former seat of Lidia Thorpe
text:
At the last federal election, the Greens suffered a catastrophic wipe-out; in the upcoming Victorian state election, they're looking to mount a comeback.

The major Greens casualties in 2025 were party leader Adam Bandt and one-time rising star Max Chandler-Mather — who even earned a rebuke from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese as he exited parliament — such was the animosity brewing between the Greens and Labor.

Now at a federal level, the Greens have a new leader in David Shoebridge, who is also keen to take the Labor vote. At the upcoming Victorian state election, that is also a primary Greens target.

David Shoebridge has declared he wants the Greens to replace Labor. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Labor holds 54 of the 88 lower house seats in the Victorian parliament, the Coalition 29, and five on the crossbench.

The Greens currently hold three lower house seats, Brunswick, Melbourne and Richmond, by comfortable margins.

They are targeting at least five more, including the Liberal-held Prahran and Labor's Footscray, Pascoe Vale, Preston and Northcote.

Greens success across this part of Melbourne could significantly erode Labor's parliamentary majority and potentially reshape the balance of power in Victoria.

Northcote is the former seat of federal senator Lidia Thorpe, who won it in a 2017 by-election.

Lidia Thorpe briefly held the seat of Northcote after a by-election in 2017. (ABC: Ian Cutmore)

Trying to take the seat back is Greens candidate Campbell Gome, a primary school teacher and trade unionist, who believes the political mood is shifting.

"We are going to keep knocking on doors, we are going to keep listening to people," Mr Gome told 7.30.

" This sense that is coming up again and again on the door is that the Labor Party has abandoned communities like ours. "

Campbell Gome lost to Labor's Kat Theophanous by just 184 votes at the 2022 state election. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Asked whether voters are enthused about Greens policies or looking to park their dissatisfaction with Labor elsewhere, he told 7.30: "I think the two go hand-in-hand."

"That's the real change in 2026 ... this sense of frustration and abandonment of [Victorian] Labor's historic position as being for ordinary people and being genuinely progressive."

In many parts of the seat of Northcote, about 7km north of Melbourne's CBD, political messaging sits alongside bustling cafes and gentrification.

Aside from its brief dalliance with Senator Thorpe, the seat has been Labor for almost a century and swung back that way in 2018.

Labor's Kat Theophanous defeated Mr Gome by just 184 votes in 2022. The looming contest is familiar territory.

Kat Theophanous says, in her view, Northcote has always been a marginal seat. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

"We expect it to be close again. For me, it's always been a marginal seat, both in 2018 and in 2022," Ms Theophanous said.

The state Labor MP rejects suggestions by her political opponents that Labor has lost touch with her electorate's progressive communities.

"I disagree with it," she said.

" I don't think we've abandoned ordinary people. I speak to ordinary people all the time, I live in this community and every day I'm showing up and listening to them and fighting for the things that they care about. "

The long-term Labor government is under pressure from across the political spectrum. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

She acknowledges some voters are tiring of the long-term Labor government but says many are concerned about a possible Coalition government.

"After 12 years, of course there's going to be people that are feeling fatigue," she said.

"I'm asking people to vote for me because of our record of delivery in the inner north."

Greens 'don't go far enough'

Recent polls of Victorian voters suggest the Greens have momentum.

After Labor replaced Jacinta Allan with Ben Carroll as premier, Redbridge and DemosAU put the statewide Greens primary vote between 14 and 17 per cent.

In Northcote though the Victorian Socialists are looking to establish themselves, and their progressive agenda could impact the Greens vote.

Victorian Socialist candidate for Northcote Kath Larkin told 7.30: "I think the main difference is that we're socialists, right? We're anti-capitalists. We oppose the system in total."

Kath Larkin is the Victorian Socialist candidate for Northcote. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

"The Greens have a politics. It's more about tinkering around the edges," she said.

" I used to vote for the Greens before we formed Victorian Socialists, but I don't think they go far enough. "

The Victorian Socialists are aiming to run candidates in every lower house seat at this election.

Like the Greens, they want to implement sweeping reforms. They are promising to freeze and cap rents, build more public housing and return essential services to public ownership, all paid for, they say, by new taxes on big corporations and the wealthy.

Like the Greens, the Socialists want to implement sweeping reforms, promising to freeze and cap rents, build more public housing and return essential services to public ownership. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Mr Gome told 7.30 the difference between the two is that the Greens are represented at every level of government and "are able to affect real change".

Ms Theophanous primarily sees the Victorian Socialists as only being a problem for the Greens.

"They are nipping at the heels of the Greens," she said.

"The Greens have some soul-searching to do about where their party stands on things, because I think that they are catering to the socialists."

In Northcote, every vote and preference matters.

Preferences matter in the seat of Northcote. (ABC News: Tara Whitchurch)

In 2022, preferences from Liberals and the Victorian Socialists largely flowed against Labor to the Greens in the seat to tighten the race. This time the Greens say they are striving to win Northcote without relying on preferences, while the Victorian Socialists are looking to influence the result.

"In Northcote, we're looking to bump up our numbers. I don't think we'll take the seat this time round," Ms Larkin told 7.30.

" [But] I think it's possible that our votes will be decisive. "

title: NSW government tables laws to allow Mount Pleasant mine expansion
text:
The NSW government has introduced laws to allow a Hunter Valley coal mine to continue operating at expanded production rates, despite a High Court ruling against it.

The operators of the Mount Pleasant mine, MACH Energy lost their High Court appeal in October, which centred on a plan to double coal extraction in the Hunter Valley until 2048.

Premier Chris Minns said the new laws being introduced would address the "unique legal uncertainty" arising from the High Court judgement.

"We're committed to our plans in relation to renewable energy and climate change, we're not walking away from it," he told reporters on Tuesday.

"But this is the biggest reform and revolution of energy markets in the state's history, and I reserve the right to make an intervention to protect jobs and grow the economy where I think it's warranted."

Mr Minns says his government is still "committed to our plans in relation to renewable energy and climate change". (ABC News)

Overriding the 'rule of law'

MACH Energy received approval for the Mount Pleasant mine expansion in 2022, but it has been tied up in legal disputes since a NSW Court of Appeal ruling last year found its approval may have been invalid, because planning authorities did not consider the overseas emissions from the exported coal.

The mine has confirmed it continued expanding even after the proceedings reached the High Court, despite the legal uncertainty surrounding its approval to do so.

In October, the High Court delivered its own decision that the expansion was invalid, because planning authorities had failed to consider the "Scope 3" emissions caused when the coal exports were burned overseas, when it approved the mine.

The mine is allowed to extract 12.5 million tonnes of coal a year. (Supplied: Nearmaps)

A lower court, the NSW Land and Environment Court, will now review the case in December.

In the meantime, the mine has to rely on its original planning permit, which allows for only 12.5 million tonnes of coal to be extracted per year, 4 million less than the 16.5 million tonnes it was on track to extract for 2026.

Mr Minns has said the bespoke laws introduced on Tuesday would authorise "an increased annual production limit of 16.5 million tonnes until 2032… consistent with their current workforce and coal production profile".

The government denied that it was in effect "overturning" the High Court decision, and said the bill would require the coal exports to go to countries that were signatory to the Paris Agreement.

Opponents believe the mining company is going behind the court process. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

But legal experts have criticised the intervention as "reprehensible" and described the government's actions as an attempt to override the "rule of law".

"The idea that a substantial mining venture can approach the government and say look, let's go behind the court processes and sort this out between ourselves is a very dangerous precedent, and that's exactly what appears to have happened here," retired judge Anthony Whealy, who is now on the board of the Centre for Public Integrity, said last month.

'It's the vibe'

The Castle actor Michael Caton, who has emerged as a supporter of the protesters. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

On Tuesday, the retired teachers who fought the High Court case gathered on the steps of NSW parliament with a range of activists and supporters, including actor Micheal Caton, from The Castle fame.

"In the last 20 years, we have doubled coal production," Caton told reporters at the event.

"We've got less than 25 years to get rid of fossil fuels, but we're doubling production of this mine up in the Hunter."

Caton said he had voted for the Minns Labor government.

"If they keep this up, they won't get my vote," he said.

Wendy Wales, the president of the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG), who opposed to the mine, said she was very disappointed the government was trying to pass legislation "ahead of a court process".

"This is a pretty dire situation, and everybody in New South Wales and Australia should be concerned," she said.

Debate on the bill has been adjourned in the lower house to a later date.

Job figures in doubt

The NSW government said MACH Energy had advised that without the legislative intervention it would need to scale back its coal production, putting "hundreds of jobs at risk".

The NSW Resources Minister Courtney Houssos said on Tuesday that "as a practical and a sensible government, we weren't prepared to stand by and see 400 workers and their families suffer the consequences of this uncertainty".

The ABC has contacted MACH Energy to ask for clarification around the figure, but it did not respond to written questions.

MACH Energy received approval for a planning modification to its original permit earlier this year to allow it to extract 12.5 million tonnes per year until 2032 — a separate approval to the expansion before the High Court.

The government says hundreds of jobs would be at risk. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

In that application the company stated that it would continue to employ 575 personnel, until the permit's expiration in six years' time.

The documents state that this would be a "reduction of around 125 employees" compared to the workforce relied on if the bigger planned expansion before the courts was allowed to take place.

The Mining and Energy Union claimed in October that Mount Pleasant supported "826 permanent employees and contractors" but did not provided a breakdown of that figure.

The union has also claimed reverting to the former 12.5 million tonne limit "could cost 370 jobs by Christmas", without specifying whether those jobs are direct, permanent, or contractors.

Tony Lonergan, from the DAMSHEG group, said he wanted to know where the 400 jobs figure had come from.

"When were these people hired? What are their jobs?

"It seems like blackmail to me," Mr Lonergan said.

The ABC has sent written questions to Ms Houssos about the discrepancy in the jobs figures.

Debate on the bill has been adjourned in the lower house to a later date.

title: CFMEU tried to 'sabotage' Qld safety complaints overhaul, inquiry told
text:
A former Queensland department chief has accused the CFMEU of sabotaging a workplace safety complaints overhaul, describing the union's interference as "completely off the scale".

Michael De'Ath, who served as director-general of the Department of Education, Industrial Relations and Racing under former senior Labor minister Grace Grace between 2021 and 2024, has given evidence at the commission of inquiry into the Queensland branch of the CFMEU.

The probe into alleged misconduct is re-examining allegations the union "captured" Workplace Health and Safety Queensland (WHSQ) under the former Labor government to advance its industrial agenda — a practice previously described during proceedings as a form of "institutional corruption".

Counsel assisting Dimitri Ternovski said a key focus of this week's hearings would be establishing how far the union's alleged influence extended into the upper ranks of government.

The inquiry heard the CFMEU fiercely resisted changes to how workplace safety complaints were made. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Mr De'Ath has been grilled over claims the CFMEU had a direct line to senior bureaucrats and ministers, bypassing normal workplace safety reporting procedures.

Central to the questioning was evidence from former Office of Industrial Relations [OIR] deputy director-general Kym Bancroft in June, who detailed her efforts to shut down the union's so-called "hotline" to the regulator.

Ms Bancroft told the inquiry she sought to introduce a centralised triage system, directing safety concerns through a dedicated hotline number instead of government officials.

'Most extreme obfuscation'

Ms Bancroft said the CFMEU fiercely resisted the overhaul, insisting it would continue contacting her directly.

The arrangement posed safety risks by adding an unnecessary layer to the complaints process with Ms Bancroft unavailable around the clock, the inquiry heard.

Mr De'Ath described the union's opposition as "incredibly frustrating", accusing it of intentionally trying to derail the reforms.

"This was the most extreme obfuscation of anything in my entire career, completely off the scale for a stakeholder," Mr De'Ath told the inquiry.

"[It was] quite a deliberate attempt to sabotage a process that they clearly did not want."

"I've worked in multiple jurisdictions with multiple stakeholders over multiple portfolios, if you had it on a scale of 1 to 9, the worst I would've encountered might've been a three — this is a nine," he said.

Former bureaucrat's sacking under scrutiny

Ms Bancroft also claimed she was sacked by Mr De'Ath in 2023 during which he allegedly told her that "a union group" was not "happy" with her.

On Tuesday, Mr De'Ath took sole responsibility for her termination, citing a breakdown in trust and confidence and concerns about her competence and honesty.

Qld CFMEU inquiry hears dog poisoning allegations The director of a private security business has told Queensland's CFMEU inquiry he discovered a tracking tag attached to his vehicle.

"The decision to dismiss her was your decision alone and no one else's … you stand by that?" Mr Ternovski asked.

"Ultimately, that decision is mine," Mr De'Ath replied.

Mr De'Ath was also asked about the redeployment of ex-WHSQ compliance director Helen Burgess who was considered a key link between the union and regulator.

His repeated inability to recall details surrounding the move sparked a tense exchange with Commissioner Stuart Wood KC, who questioned his account, saying it seemed "very unlikely to be true".

title: Empty chair at bed shortage summit highlights state–federal tensions
text:
South Australia's worst-ever ambulance ramping hours in August would have been reduced by two-thirds had there been no aged care bed block, the state government has argued at a health meeting intended to increase pressure on Canberra.

SA Health Minister Blair Boyer presented the modelling at a meeting of state government, health and union officials in Adelaide this morning, amid tensions with the federal government over the national shortage of aged care beds.

Those tensions were on full display in the form of an empty chair set aside for the federal Aged Care Minister Sam Rae, who was unable to attend but whose absence was made more conspicuous by a vacant space bearing his name between SA Premier Peter Malinauskas and SA Ambulance Service CEO Rob Elliott.

Short notice and a scheduling conflict were cited by the federal government for minister Sam Rae's absence from the SA government's meeting. (ABC News)

In August, ambulance ramping hours in South Australia hit 5,891, the highest on record and more than double the highest monthly figure reached under the Liberal government that was defeated by Mr Malinauskas's Labor at the 2022 state election.

Prior to that victory, Labor had prominently promised to "fix the ramping crisis", and has since repeatedly blamed consistently high ramping on a shortage of federal aged care beds for patients transferring out of hospital care.

Mr Boyer told the meeting, entitled the "federal aged care crisis", that the number of patients in public hospital beds who were unable to transfer to aged care beds was currently around 500 and could further increase to almost 700 during next year's winter peak.

He said modelling showed ramping hours would have been slashed this year had those beds been available.

"What if we had, magically, all that capacity back? What if today the system had the 500 beds, that are out of action, available to us again?" he asked rhetorically.

"One of the most powerful stats we have is the winter demand period we've just had, where it almost peaked at 6,000 hours — and would have been below 2,000 hours had we had all the capacity available to us.

" It is an extraordinary number of hours that are lost by this capacity not [being] available to us. "

Blair Boyer says his take on the aged care crisis is unlikely to win him any friends in Canberra. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Funding for aged care beds

Earlier, Mr Boyer told 891 ABC Adelaide that federal minister Sam Rae had been invited to the meeting but that "he couldn't make it".

The ABC understands the minister was only given a few days' notice of the meeting and that a scheduling issue prevented his attendance but a counteroffer was made to meet with Mr Boyer in Canberra.

The federal government has defended its aged care spending record, saying it was "not wasting a moment" to bring new residential aged care beds "online".

"Earlier this year, we announced the outcomes of an Expression of Interest process which will unlock $134.5 million to deliver 268 new residential aged care beds across five Adelaide sites, improving access to care and helping ease hospital discharge pressures," a spokesperson said.

"We're supporting the construction of around 5,000 additional residential aged care beds each year."

The state government said double that number was needed.

The SA government met with health and union officials today. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

But the federal government also said the states had knocked back opportunities to contribute to solutions.

"When states told us delayed discharge was their biggest pressure point, we listened and put $2 billion on the table ringfenced for aged care services, through the National Health Reform Agreement. The states rejected it and took the money for hospitals instead," the federal spokesperson said.

Asked whether he was doing political damage to his federal Labor colleagues by being outspoken on the issue, Mr Boyer replied: "I doubt it's winning me any fans.

"Do I sit back because I'm afraid of being a bit unpopular with some of my colleagues and pull my punches? I'm not going to do that," he said.

SA Labor has pivoted from health to housing If Labor's 2022 campaign was all about ambulance patients locked out of hospitals, then 2026 is all about young people locked out of home ownership.

State opposition health spokesperson Jack Batty said today's meeting was welcomed provided it did not turn "into another talkfest".

"We really need more than summits, we need commitments, we need deadlines, we need actual results," he said.

"So often this minister's default response to really serious policy challenges is another round table or a summit. He had a crisis summit last week about this."

Mr Malinauskas likened the high demand on aged care beds to a freight train that been in motion for "decades" and had "now arrived at the station".

"The country's not ready for it," he told Radio National earlier today.

"There are a range of decisions that were made frankly during the course of the Abbott years that unwound various policy measures that had been introduced to prevent this from occurring and the consequences of it are now playing out."

title: Backflip on deadline to release plan to attract clinicians into Qld health system
text:
Queensland's health minister has backflipped on a deadline to release a plan to add tens of thousands of new employees to the health workforce.

An analysis released a year ago today revealed the state needed 6,000 new doctors and 46,000 health workers by 2032.

A workforce plan to map out how Queensland would deliver those clinicians was due to follow.

In August, Health Minister Tim Nicholls said the plan was being finalised and would be released "a little later this year".

But asked today in Rockhampton, the minister said there was no timeline for its release.

"No, we want to get it right. And getting it right is not a deadline for a headline, which was the modus operandi of the former government," Mr Nicholls said.

"When we've concluded all of that investigation, we'll have a proper workforce plan that people can have faith in, and that will deliver the workforce in the places we need it, when we need it."

Regional disparity

The workforce analysis showed a disparity in healthcare workers between regional and metro areas.

In some allied health professions, regional workforce gaps were as high as 50 per cent, and 72 per cent of workforce growth had occurred primarily in metro areas.

AMA Queensland president Associate Professor Erica Gannon said a workforce plan would be vital in addressing shortfalls.

Erica Gannon says demand for health services is only going to increase. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"The workforce gap analysis was a positive first step in developing a sorely needed, system-wide workforce plan," she said.

"Regional and remote Queenslanders will suffer the most without a comprehensive plan to get more doctors into the system.

"We know demand for health services is only going to increase given our growing and ageing population, coupled with improved but often expensive medical technologies used to treat increasingly complex conditions."

The analysis also showed a fifth of Queensland's registered health workforce was approaching, or at, retirement age.

Opposition Leader Steven Miles called for the urgent release of the plan to attract the necessary workers.

"The best time for a workforce plan was a year ago. The second best time is today," he said.

Steven Miles has called for the urgent release of the plan. (ABC News)

"It's now been a year today since the LNP promised a health workforce plan, and in that year, all we have heard from them is excuses."

Mr Nicholls assured the work was ongoing.

"We're doing the proper planning around the workforce plan, but we're not letting the grass grow under our feet."

It comes as Training Minister Ros Bates announced an expansion to the government's free nursing program, with a further 2,000 TAFE places available.

title: CFMEU promised 'positive outcomes' to Big Build contractor, inquiry hears
text:
A senior figure in a major construction company has told the royal commission into Victoria's Big Build he was promised there would be "positive outcomes" for future projects if his company aligned itself with the CFMEU.

This week's hearings have focused on events related to a work stoppage at a level crossing removal project in Melbourne's north, which was contracted to the John Holland construction company.

In 2022, work ceased on the Gap Road project on June 6 and resumed on June 7 after control of the site was transferred to the CFMEU (Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union).

The commission heard that project costs blew out by an estimated $6 million.

John Holland's Steve Testolin has given evidence about a meeting at the CFMEU headquarters during a crucial stoppage on the Gap Road level crossing removal project. (Supplied)

The second day of the hearing focused on dozens of incidents where CFMEU organisers raised safety concerns to gain entry to the Gap Road site, including 31 times on the week before the June 6 stoppage.

John Holland's general superintendent Steve Testolin told the royal commission he did not believe there were any valid safety issues on site and that he suspected the union had another agenda.

"April, May, there were continual requests to enter sites … it was more of an intelligence-gathering mission," Mr Testolin said.

He said the Gap Road site was the only level crossing removal project not aligned with the CFMEU.

Victorian commission hears CFMEU influence 'unprecedented' Public hearings started with the events leading up to a stop-work at a Sunbury site in 2022.

He told the hearing about being summoned to a meeting at CFMEU's headquarters to receive the union's list of demands to resume work.

Mr Testolin said one of those present was senior CFMEU official Joe Myles.

"Joe then pretty much said, 'Enough with the small talk, what do you want?' and the room went pretty quiet and I just thought I'd just better say something so I said, 'How about you cut the bullshit and tell me what you want?'"

Mr Testolin told the hearing the union demanded John Holland employ a CFMEU-nominated health and safety representative, cease sourcing its workers through Zoom Recruitment and instead use the union's preferred BK Labour Hire, and also swap to CCL traffic management company.

He told the hearing he and the other John Holland representatives were then told that "if we aligned ourselves with the union than there'd be positive outcomes and we'd be looked at favourably for future projects".

When asked which projects the union was referring to, he answered: "Airport rail. We'd be one of the preferred contractors."

Mr Testolin told the royal commission that earlier in the day, John Holland had called WorkSafe and the police for help when negotiations with the CFMEU about the stoppage could not be resolved.

"WorkSafe was not prepared to come out immediately so at that point which was getting into the afternoon we requested police intervention.

"They were reluctant to come out as well, believing it was an [occupational health and safety] matter.

" As pressure and level crossings became more of a CFMEU-dominated area, we were being left to fend for ourselves. "

Mr Testolin said John Holland also felt abandoned by the government representatives involved in the infrastructure project.

"Our safety records were above board but I knew that eventually we would have to concede [to aligning with the CFMEU] because we weren't being supported by authorities.

"We were pretty much being left standing alone."

Dozens of disruptions by CFMEU before stop work

Earlier, crane operator Glenn Tyrrell told the royal commission he had been employed on the Gap Road project through Zoom Recruitment and was voted in by his colleagues as the site's health and safety representative during an election.

He said there was not much of a union presence at the Gap Road project until after April 2022 after which, at times, up to four CFMEU organisers would turn up and present John Holland site management with safety concerns.

"They'd just come on site and literally stop the whole job," Mr Tyrrell told the hearing.

"They'd have their [Right of Entry] paperwork and they'd stand in front of machinery and plant and just tell the operator that he must stop."

Glenn Tyrrell gives evidence about his experiences with the CFMEU on the Sunbury Gap Road rail infrastructure construction site. (Supplied: Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects)

The commission heard that between May 25 and 31, the CFMEU issued 8 safety notices to John Holland.

It presented another 23 notices between June 1 and 2.

Mr Tyrrell described instances where union representatives would walk in front of cranes and even sat on concrete barriers that were about to be lifted into place to force the work to stop.

"Sometimes either the whole job site was shut or a certain area of the job was shut," Mr Tyrrell said.

He gave evidence that about a week after the June 6 stoppage, about 15 casual workers who had been hired through Zoom Recruitment were called into a lunch room and told they had to stop working for the labour hire firm and transfer to a new company, BK Labour Hire.

He said they were also told they were now required to join the CFMEU.

"That's the first time I joined any union," Mr Tyrrell told the hearing.

He said he had to make a bank transfer of $590 to the union up-front for half-yearly fees.

He said he was not given any reason why the casual workers had to transfer to the new labour hire company.

John Holland's site supervisor Robert Van Den Tol told the hearing he had several decades experience before the Gap Road job, where safety was part of his responsibilities.

He said he had always considered it to be a safe worksite and that he did not believe the CFMEU made any substantial improvements once the union took control of the site and installed its own safety representative.

He told the royal commission he did not agree with the union's claim of a problem with risk assessments for piling works that resulted in the June 7 stoppage.

"Definitely not because if I had seen it, I would have stopped it," he said.

"No one could start work without a Safe Work Methods Statement. No one."

Robert Van Den Tol gave evidence to the royal commission via video link. (Supplied: Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects)

Mr Van Den Tol said that when union officials had been entering the site, they often did not follow proper procedure, such as signing in, alerting John Holland to their presence and waiting until their Right of Entry permits had been handed in.

He said they were not supposed to be wandering around the worksite without an escort if they had not undergone a site induction.

"Not supposed to, no. Did they? Yes."

Mr Van Den Tol agreed under questioning that the union officials were swearing at him and making derogatory comments during the June 6 stoppage.

"Their attitude to me was, well I won't tell you the words…"

The hearing continues.

title: 'You can't fix this': Navigating the grief of losing a child
text:
Our recent story about parents who have experienced the loss of a child struck a chord with many readers, who then shared their own journey with us.

This is how they've navigated the grief.

'Grateful for having him in our lives'

Troy — 51

"Five years ago, my son Kurtis went to sleep and didn't wake up.

He was 10 years old.

I get asked all the time, "How do you live with not knowing what happened?"

But the way I look at it is simple. What if they told you it was something that you could have avoided? How would your life be?

I'm not super religious, but I just think if God needed someone for a little job, they chose the right kid.

When I get up to heaven and see him again, I'm going to be so proud of him.

Troy and his younger son Henderson create a public art memorial for Kurtis each year. (Supplied)

I do things that help keep me connected with Kurtis. I swim, I watch videos of him, I talk about him a lot.

We used to skateboard together all the time. One day, I did the same lap of the path 80 times with tears in my eyes. I didn't care what people thought.

I also needed to get out of my job in real estate because I didn't know how to get on the phone and pretend to be happy.

My younger son Henderson and I also build an art memorial each year on Kurtis' anniversary, and we leave it there so people can see it and get to know him.

For anyone who's trying to support someone that's going through this grief, you just need to understand that you can't fix it.

You've got to let people be.

You'd be better off spending time helping them fold clothes. All the basics are the hard things to keep up with when you're going through it.

And if you're the one grieving, base yourself around the people who are helpful and stay away from ones who are negative."

'We light a candle for him each month'

Geoff — 69

"My wife and I lost our son Andrew on Christmas Eve, in 2021, when he and a friend were electrocuted in an accident on a property near Goulburn.

Andrew, who was 31, was due to get married some weeks later.

Every morning I would wake up after Andrew's death and my body would have to relive the pain.

This went on for two and a half years. It was exhausting.

Andrew Dornan died in 2021 in an electrical accident. (Supplied)

I think my wife and I were both very fortunate because people really did embrace us.

We were supported, and people listened to us in our grief.

I was encouraged by my family to go back to work as a church minister after having six months off.

Work really helped because it distracted me, and distraction is important.

Having experienced that grief gave me an insight which I didn't otherwise have.

I can sit with someone and intuitively understand their pain in a way that I couldn't before.

It's a loss you have to somehow embrace.

[Embrace] is an odd word to use and that's why I use it, because I think in a sense I had to embrace the death of Andrew, I had to accept it.

We light a candle for him on the 24th of each month.

Needless to say, those times are hard.

My wife and I simply close the front door and keep to ourselves on those days."

'There are always going to be triggers'

Anne (not her real name) — 64

"My teenage daughter died on the way to a sports tournament 20 years ago in Tasmania.

It still impacts me when I hear about a young person who has died.

One of the worst things was dealing with the media and public voyeurism. I had a call from a reporter less than an hour after she died.

The more people want to know, the more pressure there is on families to give information.

I was told two years after it happened, 'You should be getting over it by now.'

Supporting someone who's lost a child Women who have lost children talk about continuing in the wake of such grief, and how people stepped up, or stepped away.

But someone doesn't just stop grieving. There's always going to be triggers — every birthday, every Christmas, every Easter.

It's a very hollow thing to go through.

We are all different and therefore deal with grief in different ways.

If you wanted to talk to someone about it, the simple question is, 'Is it OK to ask you some questions about your child or your grief?'

I love talking about my daughter with her friends and family as it keeps her alive in my memory.

We need to talk about death more so we can cope better when someone dies.

There are countries that celebrate death. It seems strange, but I think it's healthy.

If you go and talk to a professional about your grief, or someone from a support group, if you don't click with them, that's OK, but don't stop there.

Because that's what happened to me, I went, 'This doesn't feel right.'

I think it's really important to follow up and not be scared to try again.

I found talking to someone who I connected with really important, and I still do it."

title: Justice system criminalising mental illness, psychiatrists say
text:
Australia's peak psychiatrists' body has backed calls to transform mental health care in NSW prisons, including an end to isolating suicidal prisoners in so-called "safe cells".

It follows an ABC investigation into mentally ill inmates who have died after being isolated in a safe cell, purportedly for their own protection.

Readers are advised that this article includes the names and images of Indigenous people who have died, used with family permission.

"Safe cells are a custodial response rather than a health response," Dr Ian Korbel, chair of the Royal Australian New Zealand College of Psychiatrists (RANZCP) NSW branch, told the ABC.

"What people at risk of suicide should have is good, close support with nursing staff, psychologists and psychiatrists. Sometimes they might need medication.

"Often they'll need support and they'll need to be preferably in a cell with other people, rather than by themselves."

Earlier this week, forensic psychiatrist Dr Kerri Eagle called for prison health agency Justice Health, an arm of the NSW health department, to be the lead agency managing mentally ill prisoners.

"It is not appropriate for Corrective Services to be managing those health conditions because their goals are security and law enforcement," she said.

Dr Eagle is a clinical director at Justice Health but was speaking as a private practitioner.

Kerri Eagle says Justice Health workers must defer to Corrections on security matters and are only "visitors in their house". (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

Currently, at-risk inmates are assessed by a team of two CSNSW staff and one Justice Health worker, and inmates sent to safe cells are monitored by guards.

Dr Korbel agreed health workers, not correctional officers, should be assessing and monitoring prisoners with serious mental illness.

"I've worked in the prison system myself, I've seen that we have many caring and good guards that work in the system too, but they're not trained to deal with the sorts of psychiatric problems that we're seeing in prison."

Nick Espie from Aboriginal legal services peak body NATSILS said too many people were dying in prison "because they're not receiving the specialist care that they should be receiving".

He said Indigenous people were over-represented in prison and in mental health statistics and must be involved in delivering care in custody.

"We know [Aboriginal-led health programs] are more effective in working with our own people," the Arrernte man said.

"[They] should be and could be resourced properly to deliver mental health and disability services to people inside and outside of the prison space."

Nick Espie says Aboriginal-led services provide culturally safer care. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson)

In Victoria, Indigenous groups also want oversight of prison health care transferred to the health department, as recommended by the Yoorrook Justice Commission, with a model of care led by Aboriginal community-controlled health organisations (ACCHOs).

Last week, the ABC revealed that 48 NSW coronial inquests since 2015 had identified failures in the care or supervision of people with mental illness. Of these, 14 related to the death of an Indigenous person.

Mental health failures behind bars Tracy Mackander thought the coronial inquest into her son Bailey's death in custody would bring change. Instead, it brought more heartache. An ABC investigation can reveal a prison system failing its most vulnerable.

These include interim findings into the case of Tammy Shipley, a 47-year-old Aboriginal woman with schizophrenia who died from water intoxication after spending 10 nights in a monitored safe cell.

She was the third NSW prisoner with schizophrenia to die from polydipsia in less than two years, with 35-year-old Daniel Turnbull also dying in a safe cell just two months earlier.

The RANZCP wants greater focus on diverting people with severe mental illness out of the justice system and into treatment.

Dr Korbel cited a 2019 UNSW study that found NSW prisoners with psychosis who received a court treatment order rather than a sanction were less likely to reoffend.

"We see a lot of people with serious mental illness … who are homeless, living on the streets, and that puts them at risk of committing relatively minor crimes just to survive," he said.

"When they go into care, their rates of recidivism decrease, they can access supports and housing … and we can see them become functioning members of society."

Giancarlo de Vera, CEO of BEING Mental Health Consumers, said the mental health crisis behind bars followed years of under-investment in community care.

They pointed to internal NSW Health documents, released last month, which estimated there was a $600 million annual shortfall for frontline mental health staff.

"We are treating the justice system and prisons as a de facto mental health system," they said.

Giancarlo de Vera says the ABC's revelations about failures in prison mental health care are "unsurprising but equally devastating". (supplied)

Asked about Dr Eagle's comments on Monday, Premier Chris Minns defended the delivery of mental health care in NSW prisons.

"It may be not reasonable in all circumstances for a prisoner in psychological distress to be seen by a psychiatrist, at least initially," he said.

"Most of the interaction is with prison staff and is with Corrections officers and that's the nature of prison."

A Corrective Services spokesperson previously told the ABC it "adheres to strict legislative and regulatory frameworks to safely, securely and humanely manage people within its facilities".

title: Ahead of the World Cup final, Jamayne Isaako can't miss
text:
As New Zealand's Jamayne Isaako lined up his conversion attempts in the World Cup semifinal against Tonga, he did so in the middle of a hurricane while it was raining sideways.

The Kiwi winger is one of rugby league's best goal-kickers, but even he admits the horrific weather took things away from him in Newcastle.

"I had no idea where I was aiming the ball," Isaako said.

But despite the conditions, Isaako kept slotting them — into the wind in the first half and bending them through like a boomerang in the second because right now, Jamayne Isaako can't miss.

Loading Instagram content

His last kick from the sideline, when he hung the ball miles outside the right upright only for it to turn harder than even legendary New Zealand spin bowler Daniel Vettori ever managed, and go through with all his teammates there to celebrate, was his favourite, as the Kiwis stormed into the World Cup final with a 34-10 victory.

"I knew if I aimed it right, the shape would bring it back around, but I had no idea where they were going," Isaako said.

"I have a massive hook in my kick, so I aim a bit more right than most kickers, but I was just happy I got them.

"Particularly the last one, with all the boys behind me."

With the rugby league year ending after Sunday night's World Cup final, Isaako is about to finish one of the greatest-scoring seasons in the game's history.

Isaako's kicking, in atrocious conditions, was typically excellent in the semifinal win over Tonga. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

He was the NRL's top scorer in 2026, becoming just the fourth player ever to pass 300 points with his final total of 310 the third-highest single-season mark in league history.

Throw in a prolific and accurate World Cup campaign, in which he's kicked 36 goals from 38 attempts and scored personal hauls of 38 points against the Cook Islands and 26 against Fiji, and his total stat line for the season is 30 games, 26 tries and 145 goals at an 86.3 per cent success rate for a total of 394 points.

With New Zealand needing every edge they can find against Australia if they're to claim their second World Cup, Isaako's kicking form could prove crucial.

Between Cameron Munster, Reece Walsh and Kotoni Staggs, the Kangaroos have no shortage of kicking options for the final, but none of them are in Isaako's class.

Isaako's kicking could provide an edge for New Zealand in the World Cup final. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Staggs and Walsh have never spent a club season as a primary goal-kicker, while Munster, who took the tee in the semifinal win over Samoa and kicked six from eight, has a career success rate of 58.02 per cent.

Isaako, by contrast, has long been one of the NRL's elite boots and is in the kicking form of his life.

"This year has probably been the best for kicking for me," Isaako said.

"I've worked on it a lot, the last two years especially. The game is only getting quicker and if there's more tries, the two points add up quickly.

"It's something I pride myself on."

Isaako has worked closely with the legendary Daryl Halligan in the Kiwis camp each of the past four seasons, and the kicking guru likens his hook on the ball to Johnathan Thurston's.

Isaako was the NRL's leading pointscorer in 2026 for the third time in his career. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Like everyone else of a black-and-white persuasion, Halligan enjoyed Isaako's circus kicks to finish the semifinal but nominated his two strikes in the opening stanza, which gave New Zealand a crucial 12-10 half-time lead after running into the gale, as his most impressive.

"His first two kicks into the breeze in the first half were his best and he could have a bit of fun with the ones at the end when there was a bit less pressure," Halligan said.

"Jamayne is pretty similar to JT in a way with that curve. He's a buoyant guy like JT, even if he doesn't have the laugh."

Isaako credits Halligan with simplifying his kicking approach and while Halligan is quick to direct credit back to the Melbourne-bound winger, he isn't surprised to see the 30-year-old's accuracy improved as he's aged.

Australia's old power conquers the new world Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times, but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semifinal was a reminder of Goliath's power.

"There's not a lot of hard coaching this time of year, you're not going to change much and there's not much that needs to be changed," Halligan said.

"But goal-kickers get better as they get older. Why wouldn't they? They've ironed out the things they can do better.

"He makes good contact and puts a lot of work into his details. He knows where he's heading with it.

"The wind can play a factor if you want it to, but it won't change what he wants because he knows where it has to go."

History could beckon for Isaako on Sunday night in more ways than one.

He's currently level with Shaun Johnson on 225 points as New Zealand's all-time highest Test pointscorer and is all but certain to take outright possession of the record in the World Cup final.

Why the RLWC is New Zealand's to lose It took all their power and all of Kalyn Ponga's brilliance and toughness, but after getting past Tonga in Newcastle, the World Cup is within New Zealand's grasp.

But Isaako would give every one of them back in a second if it would mean a Kiwi victory.

The Christchurch man is of Samoan descent and played one Test for the Toa in 2019 but has represented New Zealand ever since because of how the country changed his family's life, a debt he feels he can never repay.

"New Zealand is where I was born and raised, and I choose the black jersey because New Zealand gave my family an opportunity, like a lot of the Pacific Island boys in this team," Isaako said.

"To win a World Cup would be a dream come true. We know what it meant to the old boys who were there in 2008, we've been fortunate enough to have a few of them come into camp and tell us their story.

"Whenever we're able to represent the black jersey, it's an honour and a privilege and for a lot of us, it's the pinnacle.

"It would be huge for us as players to win, but more for our country."

title: Greenhouse pollution down but global warming surges as climate talks begin
