Global carbon emissions are projected to decrease by 0.4 per cent this year, a new report shows, as world leaders begin to arrive at climate talks in Turkey, where the Australian president of negotiations hopes to secure agreement to speed up the electrification of the world’s economy. Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen with Queen Mary of Denmark at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey on Monday. Getty Images The fall in emissions, revealed by the Global Carbon Project, was reported alongside new data showing that August 2026 was the joint warmest month ever recorded, alongside July 2023. “With a global average surface air temperature 1.65°C higher than the estimated pre-industrial baseline, this August was the first month to exceed 1.5°C since November 2025,” says an analysis published by Copernicus, the European Union’s Earth observation program. It said August marked the end of Western Europe’s warmest summer on record, surpassing the previous record set in 2003. The fall in greenhouse gas emissions is linked to both the rapid deployment of renewable technologies and a fall in demand caused by oil prices shocks stemming from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which caused emissions from oil to fall 1.9 per cent. The Global Carbon Project, a collaboration of scientists tracking and analysing greenhouse pollution, found the dip in pollution it detected was not enough to signal a sustained declined.

Advertisement

It found that while global energy demand continues to rise, two-thirds of the increase is being met by new solar and wind power and electric vehicles. Related Article Good Weekend ‘I was hooked for life’: The moment as a teenager Chris Bowen will never forget “A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, who led the study. “The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline.” The impact of compounding energy crises caused by wars in Iran and Ukraine has roiled global climate efforts, causing demand surges for both renewables and alternative fossil energy sources, and causing governments to focus on domestic price impacts rather over global climate pledges. “This year’s fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shockwave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer,” said UN climate chief Simon Stiell in his opening speech to COP31 on Monday.

Advertisement

But the cost increases have also shifted the economic case in favour of electrification, said International Energy Agency executive director Fatih Birol, who has declared that the world is entering ‘the age of electrification.’ Related Article Climate policy 35-by-35: A catchy slogan, a mammoth negotiation and a plan to save the world “When I first said that we got a lot of eyebrows raised,” he said in an interview with this masthead earlier this month. “But the market dynamics – leaving aside climate change – confirm it every day, every year, every month.” China’s emissions over 2026 are projected to decrease by 0.9 per cent, following two years of low emissions growth. Alongside its falling oil use, China’s coal emissions rose by 0.3 per cent, but electricity generation from renewables continues to grow strongly. While China produces 32 per cent of global fossil emissions, it is also the country most active in deploying clean technologies and increasing carbon sinks through reforestation, the report found.

Advertisement

China has backed calls by the COP climate talk hosts, Turkey, and president of negotiations, Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, to seek global agreement to accelerate the electrification of the global economy. Turkey is responsible for voluntary agreements made at the United Nations climate conference, while Bowen is responsible for the formal negotiations, which demands consensus from all the 193 nations which are party to the Paris climate treaty, and the European Union. Related Article Paris Agreement UN climate talks begin amid rapid warming and global fuel shock Bowen has signalled he would like an agreement on electrification to be part of a final COP cover text, though India, the world’s third-largest greenhouse polluter, has declared opposition to the effort. The talks begin in the face of global frustration at the failure of the COP process to either halt warming or implement many of the agreements signed at previous summits. Bowen and his Turkish counterpart, Environment Minister Murat Kurum, are seeking to manage expectations for this meeting by declaring it would focus on delivering on past commitments rather than pursuing sweeping new deals and pledges. “It should be an implementation COP, because frankly speaking, we have too often fallen into the trap of trying to do many new things, rather than just deliver on what we already have,” EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra told the European Parliament in a climate debate last month.

Advertisement

The effort to attract nations to sign on to plan to increase electrification to 35 per cent by 2035 – under the slogan “35 by 35” – is seen as a way to advance ambition to decarbonise the world without engaging in a dispute with oil exporting nations like Saudi Arabia. Marnus Labuschagne believes Jack Clayton was ready to answer an SOS by the Australian Test side, as the axed batsman outlined his own plan to force his way back into the international fold. Addressing the media for the first time since the country’s selection chief, George Bailey, confirmed the Queenslander would not be considered for the forthcoming four-match series against New Zealand, Labuschagne stressed he had “no doubt” that a comeback to the Baggy Green beckoned. To achieve that, the 32-year-old knows only runs will aid his course to board the plane in time for next year’s series in India, having gone more than three years without a Test century. Marnus Labuschagne trudges off after throwing away his wicket in Gqeberha, South Africa. Getty Images His path back will start from Wednesday when he captains the Bulls’ Sheffield Shield clash against Tasmania at the Gabba. This is similar to last year, when he was dropped after the West Indies series, only to regain his place for the Ashes after scoring two centuries and a further four one-day tons.

Advertisement

“I think you use this as an opportunity to step back from the scrutiny and being under the pump for probably two years now … and really just enjoy your time here, find ways to win games for Queensland, score runs, and enjoy the game,” Labuschagne said. Related Article Australian cricket ‘Baby Barrel’: The next Boland leading Australia’s emerging cartel “I think my path back into the Australian team will work itself out. I’ve done it before, and for me, it’s something I truly want. I have no doubt I’ll get back there – when, who knows? But that’s still the aspiration and desire. “Over a long period of two years being in this limbo of in and then not doing enough, but doing just enough, has taken its toll a little bit.” Labuschagne admits he knew that without a score of note in the 2-1 series defeat in South Africa he would be on the chopping block. Having averaged just 21.83 across the campaign, he shed light on where he went wrong.

Advertisement

He insisted he felt he had been batting well, and his run of regularly surpassing 30 – as he did three times in South Africa – was symbolic of “not someone who’s not batting well; it’s someone who’s making mistakes when they’re in”. “A lot of those mistakes have potentially come from the pressure of having to keep scoring runs and being on the verge of losing my spot. When you’re thinking too much about yourself, your focus tends to go down that path and not on what the team needs,” he said. Loading “I think if you look at those dismissals in South Africa, some of those dismissals feel like they come from a lack of clarity on what the team needed, and my own personal battle with scoring runs and missing out, and getting to 30 and going ‘I really want to go on’, and trying to rush the game. “I think playing for Queensland is stepping back, finding ways to win games for Queensland, doing whatever it takes. It doesn’t matter if that’s scoring fast, slow, blocking out, it’s a real team focus.

Advertisement

“Hopefully, when I come back into that Australian lineup – obviously the only way that’s going to happen is through mountains of runs – that is the focus; getting back into that team-orientation around what do we need from me.” Related Article Test cricket Australia’s batting is under siege. An unheralded candidate has thrust his hand up A genuine bat-off to succeed Labuschagne beckons, with state teammate Clayton firmly in the frame. New South Wales rivals Kurtis Patterson and Sam Konstas, as well as South Australia’s Nathan McSweeney, will be others pushing their case. Clayton’s century last week against Victoria took him to second in the competition’s run-scorer charts (303 runs at an average of 75.75) and continued a purple patch of form dating back to the 2024-25 summer. In his 20 matches since then, he has peeled off 1408 runs at an average of 46.93. “My thing for Jack is, I’m here to support him. I understand this is the first time for him being on this journey of being in the spotlight, and whatever I can do to help him and make him feel comfortable to make sure that if he does get the opportunity, he takes it with both hands,” Labuschagne said.

Advertisement

“I think everyone’s good enough. I think it’s all this [the media attention] that is what you need to be able to deal with. I don’t think it’s the cricket, he’s skillful enough and a good player, and I think he’s got a really calm head on him as well. “He’s mature enough in his age and how he understands the game, and he’s gone through the ups and downs of Shield cricket, so there are really a lot of positives. But what I will say is it’s not just him, there are a lot of really good candidates as well.” Loading Labuschagne’s press conference came as Usman Khawaja’s book, Sabr, was released, with early snippets attracting headlines regarding the South Africa Sandpaper Gate saga of 2018. In the autobiography, Khawaja claims the entire squad – of which, Labuschagne was not a part – were aware of the use of sandpaper on the ball, with only Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft receiving long-term suspensions.

Advertisement

Labuschagne said there had been no talk in the change rooms in South Africa about what details Khawaja’s book may unveil, but believed Smith was handling the rehashing of the saga well. Related Article Australian cricket Cricket Australia refuses to re-open sandpaper scandal investigation “I think Steve’s all right, I think what’s happened is they served a pretty dear punishment for what the circumstance was – from an ICC perspective, a one-game ban is a recommendation, and they served a year of their cricketing career,” Labuschagne said. “I think whatever comes from this, they’ve certainly paid their dues for what they were involved in. I don’t think there’s anything that’s going to come up and change anything for Steve specifically. “I wasn’t there at the time, so it’s not for me to speak about.”

Page and his team are in the spotlight after the strip used for last summer’s two-day Ashes Test was rated unsatisfactory by the ICC and cost CA about $10 million in revenue. title: Clarence young guns open ‘post-Nobu’ Japanese restaurant

Eating outFood Clarence young guns open ‘post-Nobu’ Japanese restaurant The Clarence team has a lot of experience in Japanese restaurants, and they have some very specific ideas about what they should be. Next time you see Ben McShane, ask him about London restaurants. The chef and Clarence co-owner will joke about his time working in the UK capital as a form of “trauma-bonding”, and he’ll shake his head and get liberal with expletives when describing 80 hours a week in a “tiny kitchen in East London, working shoulder to shoulder” with friends such as Matt Kuhnemann and Zoe O’Mahoney. Nito opened early November just a few doors down on Fish Lane from sister venue Clarence. Morgan Roberts But he also recognises what it gave him, which, ultimately, a business partner and a longterm manager. “It’s fun as well,” McShane says. “It’s challenging and rewarding and you get a lot out of it and you become a better cook. You progress a lot as a chef and even as a person … It builds a lot of resilience and discipline and skill.

Advertisement

Related Article Brisbane’s best vegetarian sanger? This glorious thing is a contender “You’re all going through this challenging part of your life and you learn together and learn to cover for each other.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Kuhnemann co-owns Clarence and also its new sister venue, Nito, a couple of doors down on Fish Lane. O’Mahoney is managing across both venues, and Max Burns is onboard as head chef – he worked with McShane in Stokehouse Q and followed him to London with a Tenure at Two Lights when McShane was leaving that restaurant to move back to Australia. Nito’s dining room is moody and playful. Morgan Roberts Nito opened early November and the first thing you need to know is it’s very different to Clarence.

Advertisement

It’s dark and moody, its design tiered and semi-subterranean, the defining colours orange and red. Dark timber and unpainted besa brick walls are adorned with old film posters. Even the branding – “Nito” scrawled in an inky script – is grungy and fun-loving compared to the quaint playfulness of Clarence. The venue makes the most of its subterranean space beneath a car park ramp. Morgan Roberts “I’m not surprised at how it’s ended up because it’s very much a lot of conscious decisions. Everything has been thought through,” McShane says. “The vibe of it is a record player in the back bar and a big grill in this dark space underneath a car park.” McShane is these days intertwined with the narrative of Clarence but previously worked at Kiyomi on the Gold Coast, and after that Umu in London when it held two Michelin stars. More recently he did a consultancy stint working alongside Alex Yu at Sokyo Brisbane when that restaurant first opened in 2024. In short, he’s spent a lot of time around Japanese cooking. Murray Cod with tomato and kombu vierge, spring onion. Morgan Roberts

Advertisement

That large grill, powered by binchotan, is the engine of a menu overseen by Burns that often takes a bunch of farmers and suppliers the team regularly works with at Clarence but applies their produce to a completely different (albeit, similarly tight) menu with more pickles, ferments and the like. To begin, from the raw section and starters you might order a soy-pickled Neighbourhood Farm tomato tartlet with whipped ricotta and shiso, fried U8 tiger prawns with a golden curry Marie Rose sauce, a pig head katsu sando with a pickled wasabi special sauce, or trout tartare served with a wafu dressing, noritamago and rice cracker. Barbecue eel with somen rösti, pickled apple and yuzu kosho. Morgan Roberts Then there’s the yakimono section (meaning grilled or fried items), which is all large-format and designed to share. There’s a whole side of Murray cod served with a tomato and kombu sauce vierge and spring onion; Japanese-style duck claypot rice with a sun-dried tomato XO and shiitake; and a hulking five-score 850-gram Imperial Blossom wagyu T-bone served with a bone-marrow yakiniku. For drinks, O’Mahoney has written a wine list that, similar to Clarence, favours around 40 or so small-scale local winemakers. But there are also 10 sakes (expect that figure to grow) which are all “interesting and funky and have been selling a lot”.

Advertisement

Neapolitan parfait with waffle cookies. Morgan Roberts McShane and Kuhnemann have not only created a restaurant that stands in contrast to Clarence, but McShane hopes it stands in contrast to other Japanese restaurants – particularly high-end spots that he worries are caught in a “post-Nobu” rut. “I’ve seen many Japanese restaurants that go through that same kind of like path and it often feels like they lack a narrative,” McShane says. “It feels like ticking boxes, and not particularly authentic in a traditional or personal sense. Nito co-owner Ben McShane. Morgan Roberts “I love those places that have like a sense of personality where there’s something genuine about what you’re trying to do there,” McShane says. “You’re doing a Japanese restaurant, but you still want it to be of that place.”

Auric Mining has inked a deal to snap up the Iron Maiden gold project near Norseman in WA, adding a historical gold resource to its growing portfolio and potentially bolstering the ore feed pipeline for its Burbanks processing facility, currently undergoing refurbishment. Under the deal, Auric will fork out an initial $1 million in cash to acquire project owner Boomerang Mining Capital, alongside repaying up to $3 million in loans used to fund the original purchase from Accent Resources. Auric Mining is set to acquire the Iron Maiden gold project, 180km south of its Burbanks processing facility in Western Australia. A further $1 million deferred payment to Accent will be guaranteed by Auric, while the vendors could pocket another $2 million in milestone payments if Auric manages to grow the project’s JORC 2012-compliant gold resource to 150,000 ounces and then 300,000 ounces. The asset includes a historical JORC 2004-compliant mineral resource of 1.4 million tonnes grading 1.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, equivalent to 68,500 ounces.

Advertisement

‘Iron Maiden offers Auric a near-term, low-cost growth and development opportunity that can be rapidly monetised.’ Auric Mining managing director Mark English The Iron Maiden project sits just five kilometres south of the historic Norseman mining hub and 180km from Auric’s Burbanks gold processing facility, placing it well within economic haulage distance. The company says 75 per cent of the gold mineralisation sits within 50 metres of the surface, suggesting the potential for low-cost, open-pit extraction. While historical, Iron Maiden’s database contains some eye-catching high-grade intercepts pointing to significant exploration upside. Previous drilling at the project’s Iron Duke deposit returned impressive results, including 11m at a stellar 22g/t gold from 39m, with another hole delivering 19m assaying 10.51g/t gold from 28m and a third landing 10m grading a hefty 19.85g/t gold from just 16m downhole. Adding another intriguing twist to the Iron Maiden acquisition is the historic Lady Mary underground mine, where production is believed to have exceeded 26,000 ounces at grades above 20g/t gold. Lady Mary sits within the project’s western banded iron formation (BIF), while the Iron Duke and Surprise deposits occupy the eastern formation. The project also occupies a prime stretch of the Mt Henry Shear, a major geological structure running through the southern Norseman-Wiluna Greenstone Belt, immediately north of Sinclair Gold’s multi-million-ounce Mt Henry goldfield.

Despite its promising credentials, much of the Iron Maiden project has seen little modern exploration in the past two decades. Auric Mining managing director Mark English said: “The Iron Maiden Gold Project is a compelling opportunity, having seen little exploration outside the Surprise and Iron Duke resources in the last 20 years. Sitting between historical mines in Norseman and Mt Henry, the Project presents immediate exploration upside and potential future feed for Burbanks.” The acquisition fits neatly into the company’s stated “hub-and-spoke” strategy of transforming from an explorer into an integrated mining house. Auric is working to re-establish the Burbanks processing facility as a 600,000-tonne-per-annum hub. Securing an ore pipeline is critical to that plan. Just last month, the company completed the Union Jack project near Coolgardie, boosting its global mineral resource inventory by 51 per cent to 301,000 ounces. That 102,000-ounce resource sits just 15km from Burbanks, providing another potential ore source for the centralised mill. Auric has demonstrated a knack for shrewd deal-making in building out its processing capability. The company recently snapped up a substantial infrastructure package for the bargain-basement price of just $1.2 million. Management says buying equivalent new equipment would likely have cost between $15 million and $20 million, putting some serious daylight between the purchase price and replacement cost.

Management has proven its ability to execute on projects. Its Munda starter pit was an exceptionally successful campaign, producing 8886 ounces of gold and outperforming predictions by a whopping 46 per cent. The operation delivered record revenue of $44.8 million and a net profit after tax of $19.3 million for the half-year to June 2026. Additionally, Auric’s joint venture with BML Ventures at the Jeffreys Find gold mine was another lucrative development, turning an initial investment of $1.2 million into a remarkable $16.5 million cash return. These successes have helped swell Auric’s war chest, with the company now holding $33.05 million in cash at the end of the September quarter and no corporate debt. Armed with plenty of cash at bank, a clear hub-and-spoke strategy centred around its own processing facility and a growing portfolio of assets within trucking distance, the company appears to be steadily assembling the key components for a long-life gold operation. The historical numbers at Iron Maiden certainly make for compelling reading. Throw in management with a track record of turning gold assets into cash and the market will likely be watching closely to see whether Auric can work its magic again and turn the project’s high-grade promise into another golden payday. title: 'I would not tolerate it': Joyce responds to alleged One Nation racial slur
text:
in brief The allegation was made was by sacked former One Nation staffer Charles Swindon.

Barnaby Joyce said such a comment would not be "acceptable" but would not place further weight on an "allegation".

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce says the alleged use of a racial slur against an Indigenous journalist would be unacceptable, but questions the veracity of the uncorroborated claim.

Nine Newspapers has reported the allegation that an unnamed person in One Nation headquarters was watching leader Pauline Hanson's televised National Press Club address in June and yelled out that NITV journalist John-Paul Janke was a "black c--t" as he asked Hanson his question.

The allegation came from sacked former One Nation staffer Charles Swindon, who said he was at One Nation headquarters at the time and witnessed the incident.

Swindon was credited with a senior role in the campaign to elect One Nation MP David Farley to federal parliament, but has since been fired.

"Mr Swindon has left the party and people have to make their conclusions about whether this can inspire a form of resentment," Joyce told SBS News.

"I was not there; I was at the press club, and this is a story I cannot corroborate. A story that doesn't stand up I am always very sceptical about. It needs to be seen in terms of exactly what was said, if it was said."

The party's treasury spokesperson said it was difficult to comment on a hypothetical situation and he was wary about giving it more oxygen.

"All I can make a comment on is an allegation. It's almost like a hypothetical," Joyce said.

"In terms of that hypothetical, it is not something that is acceptable; if a person said that around me, I would say, 'You cannot talk like that.'

"I have also said in the past to people, 'You can't talk like that, you can’t think like that.'

Joyce said he also wanted to address critics who say One Nation's policies on Indigenous spending are racially divisive.

One Nation wants to abolish the National Indigenous Australians Agency and scrap all specific Indigenous welfare programs.

"I don’t think there is a view of racism inside One Nation, there is definitely a view about stronger oversight on the spending of money," Joyce said.

"We have a view of inequality, people who are treated differently because of the colour of their skin. People should be helped because of the situation they find themselves in, there are also white people who are facing poverty.

"I reckon I know vastly more about life in Aboriginal Australia than the vast majority of other non-Indigenous people in Australia."

Hanson's office was approached for comment but declined to respond, instead directing SBS News to One Nation headquarters, which has not yet responded to questions.

title: Anthony Albanese announces mandatory reporting after OpenAI's Medicare breach
text:
In brief Anthony Albanese said the government had accepted all recommendations of a rapid review into the breach.

The safeguards would include mandatory reporting of AI risks and the independent evaluation of frontier AI models.

Artificial intelligence companies will have to abide by new "mandatory" safeguards when operating in Australia, and a regulator will be established to enforce them, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced.

The measures would include "mandatory" reporting of AI security breaches and potential breaches of criminal law, as well as the independent evaluation of frontier AI models, Albanese told reporters on Tuesday.

The AI safety regulator will be tasked with implementing measures to keep the booming industry in check and will be able to impose penalties on AI companies that violate the rules.

The measures will form part of the federal government's upcoming AI safety regulation.

The government also released findings from a review into the breach of a Medicare statistics website by an OpenAI agent earlier this year.

title: New Airbnb rules: What the changes mean for hosts and travellers
text:
IN BRIEF From 20 November, Airbnb is changing its rules to limit what hosts can ask guests to do before check-out.

Unexpected rules and requests after booking or during a stay have reportedly left some guests feeling misled.

Being faced with an endless list of chores when it's time to check out of your Airbnb stay isn't the best way to end a holiday.

Facing complaints from travellers, Airbnb is changing the rules to limit what hosts can ask guests to do before check-out. The new policy starts on 20 November.

What do the changes mean for hosts?

From November 20, hosts will need to re-check and revise their check-out chores to ensure they are simple and reasonable — and not "onerous".

For instance, they could ask guests to place used dishes in the sink rather than washing them, or gather towels in a designated place rather than launder them. This may help to avoid guest complaints and action from the platform.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The company suggests hosts should fully disclose their updated house rules and requests on the property page before guests get to the booking page.

Unexpected rules and requests after booking or during the stay can leave guests feeling misled, which can result in poorer stay experiences, bad reviews or complaints to the platform.

READ MORE The Bali venues taking a stand against bad tourist behaviour

The changes may also leave hosts with more cleaning to do. If so, hosts need to ensure they have adjusted their cleaning fee to reflect the actual cost.

However, they should also check whether their total price remains competitive compared to similar properties in the area.

What do the changes mean for travellers?

Travellers can expect a better check-out experience during their stay due to less time-consuming check-out chores.

However, while they are not required to perform work normally handled by a professional cleaner, they must still be responsible guests and leave the property in reasonable condition.

One practical tip for travellers is to always check the house rules and requests before booking.

They should keep a record, such as a screenshot or photograph, of any unexpected rules and requests introduced after the booking or during the stay. This can help if they need to report a problem to the platform.

Travellers should also be prepared for possible price increases. Some hosts may face higher cleaning costs if they can no longer rely on guests to complete certain tasks.

They may pass these additional costs on to travellers through higher cleaning fees or nightly rates.

Why have these changes been made?

Guests have questioned why they should pay a cleaning fee while still being expected to complete cleaning tasks themselves before checking out.

From their perspective, the problem is not simply how difficult each task is, but whether the overall exchange appears fair.

Guests may accept a cleaning fee when they believe it relieves them of the labour required to prepare the property for the next guest.

READ MORE The grim news for Australian travellers quietly updated this week

However, when the fee comes with a demanding list of chores, they may perceive the arrangement as less fair, as they may feel they are paying twice, once with money and again with their labour.

The new changes are therefore intended to create a fairer division of responsibilities and protect the guest experience on Airbnb.

Keeping both sides happy

Airbnb is a service platform whose value depends on both guests and hosts. This means Airbnb must consider whether the new changes are fair to both groups.

So far, the changes have sparked strong opposition from hosts.

They have called for a booking blackout on 20 November by closing their properties to new bookings, and started an online petition asking Airbnb to reconsider the rules.

The petition has attracted more than 27,000 signatures.

READ MORE Australians love traveling to the UK. They could soon be paying more

This response highlights the challenge Airbnb faces. A policy change that makes check-out easier for guests could leave hosts feeling neglected and with less control over their properties.

This may simply shift dissatisfaction from guests to hosts.

In response, some hosts may reduce their dependence on Airbnb by listing their properties on other platforms.

If enough disgruntled hosts switch completely to other platforms, it will risk the supply of properties on Airbnb and make the platform less attractive to guests.

What alternatives could Airbnb consider?

Rather than introducing policies that improve guest convenience at the expense of hosts, one possible way Airbnb could address this issue is to increase cost transparency to promote fairness to both guests and hosts.

For example, Airbnb could reintroduce a breakdown of cleaning fees in the pricing details. Hosts would need to explain how the fee is calculated and which cleaning services it covers.

This would help guests understand what they are paying for and what, if anything, they are still expected to do.

title: 'I thought I was going to die': The Australian story of 'harms' being told to the world
text:
In brief Australia is playing a key role at COP31 in Türkiye, with Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen acting as president of negotiations.

Ten Australians launched a case against the government in June, arguing it has a legal duty to protect people from climate harm.

Melissa Fisher says there was one night in her former home when the temperature crept past 35C, and she thought she was "going to die".

"I was so overheated. I started feeling very sick and drowsy and dizzy," she says.

"I started to panic that my brother would find me the next day and I would not be here because of how hot it was."

Fisher was living in a public housing unit in northern Adelaide at the time with no insulation, only concrete walls and a tin roof. She has since moved to another unit with temperature control.

She says there was "no sleeping" when heat lingered overnight in her last home and no relief because she couldn't take showers to cool off, due to a painful inflammatory skin condition.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Fisher is one of 10 claimants from across the country who launched a human rights case against the Australian government earlier this year, arguing it has a legal duty to protect people from climate harm.

The Hard Truths case

Known as the 'Hard Truths' case, the group, including First Nations people, firefighters and people living with disabilities, argue climate change is already causing them "devastating harm" and that the government's approval and subsidisation of coal and gas projects are fuelling escalating risks.

They outlined broad-ranging effects of climate change across the country, including floods, the Black Summer bushfires, the South Australian algal bloom and extreme heat.

According to their submission, by failing to regulate fossil fuel production in line with climate targets, the Australian government is violating the group's human rights, including the rights to life, privacy, family and home life, and culture.

Represented by the Human Rights Law Centre, Environmental Justice Australia and Earthjustice, they called on the United Nations Human Rights Committee to declare Australia's approval and subsidisation of coal and gas projects unlawful.

Mel Fisher (front left) said she is grateful claimants from the Hard Truth case could represent the group at COP31. Credit: Environmental Justice Australia

"We send so much coal overseas to be burnt and then the government wipes their hands of it and pretends it doesn't exist because we've sent it overseas. But the fact is the world doesn't have borders for gases and climate change," Fisher said.

According to Naru Research, led by climate and energy researcher Tim Baxter, emissions from Australia's exported fossil fuels "essentially doubled" between 2005 and 2020, while it has seen some decrease in emissions produced onshore.

Now, after launching the case in June, several members of the group are heading to this year's Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), which kicked off on Monday in Antalya, southern Türkiye.

They are attending to speak directly to the Australian government and participate in formal side events.

Fisher says she couldn't attend for medical reasons, but she's thankful some representatives of the case will attend the conference to raise awareness.

Australia at COP31

Australia is playing a key role as co-host at this year's COP, with Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen acting as the president of negotiations.

However, Australia's role is being scrutinised by experts and advocates, who argue there are conflicts between its domestic policy and what it's advocating for on the global stage.

Ahead of COP31, a letter signed by more than 500 academic experts from universities and research institutes, and addressed to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, was published, outlining a "paradox at the heart of Australia's climate leadership".

The letter argued "Australia has pledged to represent its Pacific family on the world stage while advancing new and expanded coal and gas projects at home, with no plan to phase out production".

It also detailed what it called an "extraordinary convergence of events relevant to the climate crisis", including the glacier collapse in August that led to mass devastation and the deaths of more than 1,400 people in Nepal, and the announcement from the United Nations Environment Programme that 1.5C of global warming is now unavoidable.

Alina Leikin, principal lawyer from Environmental Justice Australia, told SBS News COP31 is presenting a "stark reality" for the Australian government.

"While Australia is playing this very important role, it hasn't really held up the mirror to its own policies — particularly when it comes to exports," she said.

Leikin said the claimants from the Hard Truth case are attending COP31 to relay "the catastrophic impacts of climate change" in their own lives to the global community.

Speaking to The Guardian's Australian Politics podcast last week about this criticism, Bowen said nations that export fossil fuels and those that import them are both managing energy transitions.

"Other ministers certainly recognise that Australia's doing well in its transition, that we've got great domestic decarbonisation plans in place," Bowen said.

In a statement to SBS News, the minister said COP31 is an "opportunity to show what cooperation can deliver at this crucial time for both our climate and global energy security".

"It will be about unlocking finance and investment, cheaper energy for households, accelerating electrification and boosting action on the ocean, nature's greatest climate regulator," he said.

A 'landmark' ruling sets out a path

The Hard Truths case is the first case to be filed in an international court or body against a country for climate harm since a landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) last year that paved the way for such action.

The advisory opinion delivered in July 2025 laid out obligations for states related to climate change, citing international treaties including the Paris Agreement (which set the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels) and international law, including human rights law and environmental law, including the duty to prevent significant harm to the environment.

While non-binding, the ruling clarified that even though the climate crisis has been caused by many countries and entities, the failure of states to take action to protect the climate system from greenhouse gas emissions may be an "internationally wrongful act which is attributable to that state".

Rebekkah Markey-Towler, a research fellow from Melbourne Climate Futures at the University of Melbourne, told SBS News it had broad implications for climate litigation around the world.

READ MORE Meet the young people who could outlive their own country

"It was a significant and a landmark moment in that regard to say to countries 'You have a responsibility to act on climate change and if you don't, there are going to be consequences under international law,'" she said.

Markey-Towler said the launch of a case against the Australian government was not surprising after the ICJ ruling, and Australia has been a "hotspot for climate litigation" for several decades.

Fisher says being involved in the Hard Truths case has felt "meaningful" and she takes pride in "putting pressure on the government to do more for climate change".

For now, the group is awaiting the government's response to their challenge. Fisher says she hopes they could see a pause on coal and gas activity until they get a result.

title: Australia's weapon against inflation has a side effect. Is there an alternative?
text:
IN BRIEF Some politicians are calling for alternatives to interest rates be considered to tackle inflation.

Economists say rate controls are the most effective tool.

Australia's cash rate is now at the highest it's been since the global financial crisis in late 2008 and many are feeling the pain.

With growing anxiety about the economy, whether the war in Iran will continue to drive up inflation, and the soaring cost of living, some Australians are wondering whether there are other ways to curb inflation than the "blunt instrument" of interest rate hikes.

The push for alternatives is also being fuelled by federal politicians including Greens leader David Shoebridge and independent senator David Pocock, who's calling for a "rethink on how we tackle inflation".

Pocock is pushing for a Senate inquiry to explore alternatives.

The campaign to steer away from rate rises

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Australia has used interest rates to manage inflation since the 1990s, with the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) aiming to keep it between 2 and 3 per cent. Lifting rates is intended to reduce house prices and household spending, and affects the exchange rate by reducing domestic spending.

But some say it's not effective in the current environment.

The left-leaning Australia Institute think tank says the main driver of inflation today is soaring fuel prices prompted by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz — something which the RBA has no control over.

"It doesn't matter whether they put them up as they did to 4.85 per cent, they put them up to 5 per cent, they put them up to 10 per cent, they put them up to 20 per cent — that is going to do nothing to open the Strait of Hormuz," Australia Institute senior economist Matt Grudnoff said in a recent podcast.

"They're not connected in any way."

He also pointed to the inflationary impact of the growth of AI data centres, something the RBA has acknowledged. Demand for workers, material and land, as well as water and electricity, is coming at a time when the economy is operating at close to capacity.

"These two big forces that are pushing inflation, Australian interest rates will do nothing to impact them," Grudnoff said.

Pocock has put forward terms of reference for a Senate inquiry to look into alternatives to rate hikes. It hasn't yet been agreed to by parliament.

"There has to be a better way, and I've had so many Canberrans and people across the country writing and saying, 'hang on, this is madness, we have to find a better way to find a few more levers to pull and control inflation'," he told ABC News last week.

Greens leader David Shoebridge is also pushing for alternatives, saying: "It's time for a different approach, one that actually takes into account the real drivers of inflation: AI data centres, illegal wars and the 1 per cent."

What are the alternatives to rate hikes?

There are a number of levers available, including targeted tax increases, cutting government spending or lifting compulsory super contributions.

Raising the GST would be another option to stem consumption, but experts say it won't be as effective because it doesn't impact asset prices or the exchange rate. Then there's the hurdle of getting it cleared by various levels of state and federal parliaments, and regulatory monitoring to ensure businesses aren't profiteering.

"It sounds nice in theory, but it would probably be very impractical to put into play in reality," macroeconomist Luke Hartigan from the University of Sydney told SBS News.

Another option is the super guarantee — by lifting compulsory contributions.

"What it means is that people will put more money into their savings account ... if we wanted to take some heat out of the economy," Hartigan said.

"Again, it only affects the one channel of monetary policy, that cash rate, the cash flow channel; it won't affect the exchange rate."

He also said this alternative may not be fair on younger people who are more likely renting.

"The other thing is we don't know what will happen or how much we need people's incomes to go up or down," Hartigan said.

Another option is targeted tax increases on certain populations — for example, older homeowners who may be shielded from rate hikes. That too, Hartigan says, would only affect cash flow rather than exchange rate or asset prices.

And it's also politically difficult and would need the government to make an unpopular decision.

The political parties also have ideas. The Liberal Party argues curbing government spending would tackle inflation.

Diana Mousina, deputy chief economist at AMP, says cutting government spending would also come at a cost.

She said returning government spending to the historical average of around 23 per cent of GDP, compared to the current 28 per cent, would need around $135 billion in spending cuts.

"That would be an enormous fiscal adjustment," she wrote in a recent briefing paper.

"Cutting spending can mean fewer government services, lower payments or reduced programs, while higher taxes leave households with less disposable income.

"The pressure may fall on different parts of the economy than it does with higher interest rates, but somebody still has to spend less."

Meanwhile, Shoebridge has proposed national rent controls, halting the construction of new data centres and hiking company taxes.

Treasures Jim Chalmers has framed the government's changes to negative gearing, capital gains taxes and trusts as moves against financial inequality, whilst also acknowledging Australian households are hurting.

'No painless way out'

Mousina says there is no simple policy that allows us to bring inflation down without some economic cost.

"If inflation reflects demand running ahead of the economy's capacity to supply goods and services, ultimately demand needs to slow or supply needs to increase."

Hartigan says interest rates remain the most effective way of managing inflation.

"We don't like them, but they're better than the alternative, unfortunately," Hartigan said.

"We need to take some medicine. It's going to be bad medicine, so there's no easy way out of fixing inflation.

"There's no painless way out, unfortunately."

title: Manosphere content could get shut down, inquiry hears, amid minister's denial
text:
IN BRIEF A Senate inquiry is hearing submissions into the the government's digital duty of care bill.

Wayne Holdsworth, whose son Mac died after a sextortion scam, urged politicians not to turn online safety into a political contest.

This story contains references to suicide

New laws aiming to reform online platforms so they don't cause harm to children could "shut down the manosphere", drown businesses in red tape, and stifle free speech, an inquiry has heard.

Bereaved parents told a Senate inquiry into the government's digital duty of care bill that safer platform design and enforcement are urgently needed, but Liberal senator Sarah Henderson and tech company executives argued that new categories of harm are too broad and the bill is poorly written.

The Digital Duty of Care Bill aims to force online services, including social media platforms, search engines, apps, games, and AI chatbots, to ensure Australians enjoy a safe digital environment.

Users may be given a choice between algorithm-recommended content and a feed limited to people and pages they follow. Companies that fail to comply with the new rules could face fines of up to $109 million.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said the volume of image-based abuse reports to eSafety shows Australians are not adequately protected.

"If you build it, you are responsible for its risks," Wells told Nine's Today program on Monday, arguing the bill would establish basic safety standards and require companies to address risks in their products.

Where safety meets speech

Henderson said vague references such as "hostile attitudes towards women" could limit legitimate debate, saying Wells told her the bill was not about stopping the manosphere, but a departmental briefing suggested otherwise.

"It seems this is more about shutting down free speech than tackling harm," Henderson said. "Now the mandatory codes and standards are being removed and replaced with guidelines [made by the eSafety commissioner] that are not enforceable".

Wells previously told the National Press Club Australians could still listen to manosphere podcasts, arguing the bill wouldn't lead to government censorship.

Vague, undefined categories of material "harmful to children" or that "encourages or promotes hostile attitudes towards women or gender equality" or "encourages dangerous stunts" are problematic, tech companies and Henderson said.

TikTok's Jessika Lofstedt said the bill replaced "certainty with ambiguity and with subjectivity". She warned that platforms might over-moderate contentious material to avoid penalties.

Google and Meta also called for clearer definitions, including which recommender systems are being regulated and what new powers the eSafety Commissioner may create.

Romy Listo from Our Watch, which works to prevent violence against women, told the inquiry the bill was not about stopping people from expressing views but requiring platforms to manage risks linked to gendered drivers of violence, including content that condones violence against women or promotes rigid gender stereotypes.

"Some of the messages in the manosphere are harmful and research points to misogyny and violence towards women attitudes coming from there," Listo said.

The Free Speech Union's Ruben Kirkham, a computer scientist, questioned whether platforms could realistically monitor billions of posts each day, warning the resources required may exceed available computing capacity. He estimated the cost to run an AI detection tool across Australian content would consume 2 per cent of Australia's energy.

"The resource load to police the three billion pieces of social media content made every day … there may not actually be data centres and services sufficient to implement this," he said.

Heads Up Alliance founder Dany Elachi, founder of Heads Up Alliance, which calls for delayed use of smartphones and social media by children, said the bill was ideologically driven and warned it could be "weaponised".

"[The bill contains] manufactured input from left-leaning organisations funded by the government to lobby the government back on issues the government wants to be lobbied on," Elachi said.

Henderson questioned the Australian Computer Society (ACS) about why a café or a plumber should be subject to new obligations under the duty of care to conduct risk assessments of their online activity. ACS said it will help businesses with risk assessments.

"This level of bureaucracy for small businesses is completely unjustified," Henderson said.

Families suffer consequences of online abuse

Mia Bannister, founder of Ollie's Echo, told senators her 14-year-old son Ollie had experienced online abuse and anorexia before his death by suicide. She said harm could not always be reduced to "one post and one message".

“Ollie was a boy with anorexia," she said. "Gendered assumptions can leave boys unseen, their symptoms unrecognised and their distress dismissed."

Mia Bannister's son Ollie died by suicide after he was bullied online.

Emma Mason said her daughter Tilly experienced online bullying before her death by suicide at 15 in 2022. In one incident, a fake nude image of Tilly was shared with almost 3,000 people within hours, Mason said.

She told the inquiry that police had cited a lack of jurisdiction over Snapchat, an international company operating in Australia.

"We cannot keep asking children and families to carry the consequences of the risks that could and should have been identified earlier," Mason said. "Safety by design is mandatory in every part of the commercial world except in the digital world."

Wayne Holdsworth, whose son Mac died after a sextortion scam, urged politicians not to turn online safety into a political contest.

He said he had spoken to more than 300 groups since his son's death, adding: "We need to act now."

Platforms questioned over self-harm content

Independent senator David Pocock challenged TikTok over self-harm material on the platform, asking why content that breached its rules remained available and attracted thousands of likes.

"You big platforms turn up and absolve yourselves of responsibility," Pocock said. "Why do you allow self-harm content on your platform?"

Why, he asked, was a post with almost half a million likes trending if it went against the platform's guidelines?

TikTok representative Lofstedt said self-harm content was prohibited, but "we don't get it right every time" and offered to look at specific cases while rejecting the suggestion TikTok has a widespread problem.

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young argued users needed an independent ombudsman to challenge platform decisions and unsafe design features.

title: A suspected spy, a powerful CEO and a global contest: The Nvidia controversy explained
text:
IN BRIEF The CEO of one of the world's most important tech companies has confirmed he had an affair.

US intelligence agencies say the affair was with a Chinese spy who was sharing information.

One of the world's most powerful technology bosses is embroiled in an investigation over reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting concerns of a national security breach.

Jensen Huang, the boss of American AI chipmaking giant Nvidia, apologised for the affair in a company message, saying he had been unfaithful to his wife.

"There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

Nvidia said it would open an investigation into the reports Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort" but has denied any breaches of company secrets or national security.

The company has become one of the most significant technology firms in the world, supplying the chips that AI companies need and fuelling the exponential rise of the sector. Its 2026 revenue topped US$216 billion ($311 billion) in the last financial year.

Who is the suspected spy?

United States media has named her as Alice Huang, a former TV reporter in China and more recently a top executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

That company is one of Nvidia's biggest clients in Southeast Asia. US authorities have been looking into Megaspeed over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China.

The New York Times newspaper reported last month that US intelligence agencies determined the Chinese citizen had been feeding information to Beijing.

READ MORE Chinese AI app DeepSeek banned on all Australian government devices

It's unclear what that information was or how valuable it was.

Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment from US media.

A spokesperson for China's foreign ministry said on Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" was unsubstantiated.

What has Nvidia said about the affair?

Nvidia's board said in a statement its inquiry would examine all available information but that it had "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised".

It said its CEO was cooperating with the investigation and will remain in the job during the inquiry.

Huang has already been called on by key Republican politicians to brief Congress this month about the US media reports.

The report raises "significant national security concerns regarding [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information", the Republicans said in a letter dated 4 November.

"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."

Why is Nvidia so important?

The company is at the centre of a geopolitical contest between the US and China. Its products have become strategically important for both countries trying to outmanoeuvre the other.

China wants to establish its own chip-making industry and rely less on US products, including investing in domestic products from Huawei. It wants to set up a world-leading semiconductor industry by 2030.

The US has restricted exports of advanced chips to stem China's access to powerful AI technology, fearing its impact on weapons-making. Nvidia complies with those restrictions.

"US actions have also sought to sustain US leadership in advanced chips, related parts of the semiconductor supply chain, and computing and AI applications, while slowing China's development of competitive capabilities," a 2025 research report by foreign policy expert Karen M Sutter said.

"US actions have been grounded in concerns about PRC [People's Republic of China] efforts to build an indigenous, self-sufficient, and secure and controllable semiconductor ecosystem; and PRC military-civil fusion policies that seek to use commercial advancements in semiconductors, AI, and other technologies for military uses."

title: Why your next specialist visit could cost a lot more than expected
text:
IN BRIEF Fees to see specialist doctors have gone up by around 4 per cent in the past year.

One think tank says the share of fee-free care is falling and some fees are rising faster than inflation.

Calls are growing to penalise doctors for overcharging some of the two million Australians who pay 'extreme' fees to see specialists every year.

A new report by public policy think tank the Grattan Institute found specialist fees, including for services such as psychiatry, dermatology and paediatrics, continue to soar — some rising by almost 20 per cent in the past year.

It said 800,000 Australians a year are skipping or delaying specialist care because of cost.

Meanwhile, more than two million pay at least one extreme fee a year.

"This broken system needs an overhaul, including penalising specialists who routinely charge patients more than three times the Medicare schedule fee," the institute's report authors argued.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Which services are getting more expensive?

Across all specialist medical services, the average specialist fee has gone up by 4 per cent, on top of inflation, in the last year.

Seeing a dermatologist for the first time is now 7 per cent more expensive than a year ago. For psychiatry, it's now 20 per cent more expensive than last year, which means fees are going up by about $50 a year.

READ MORE More Australians are seeing a GP. What happens next is becoming more complex

Some specialists charge more than their peers — the most expensive 5 per cent of psychiatrists charge a median out-of-pocket fee of $669 for an initial consultation. For high-cost paediatricians, it is $362. For high-cost cardiologists, it is $265.

While some services receive a partial government subsidy through the Medicare Benefits Schedule, Grattan says patient fees have "skyrocketed", and the share of fee-free care is falling. It said some fees are rising faster than inflation.

Why are specialist fees so high?

Doctors' groups say they shouldn't be blamed for the soaring costs of providing specialist services.

The Australian Medical Association blames inadequate Medicare rebates, private health insurer benefits, case complexity, geography, and workforce supply for the out-of-pocket fees.

Grattan doubts doctors' claims that fees are rising because government funding hasn't kept up with the costs of providing care, or because of costs such as staff, equipment, insurance, and rent.

It said the "real problem" is an unrestrained market with no controls on fees, which it said has been left on "autopilot" for too long.

For example, it said government rebates rose by 8.7 per cent in the past three years, but were "dwarfed" by the 30.6 per cent rise in specialist fees over the same period.

While median costs per business grew by 30 per cent overall, profits grew 70 per cent.

"Patients rarely choose their specialist, cannot easily judge the quality of care, and often cannot find out the price they will pay until they have booked their appointment, or even until they get the bill," it said.

What can be done to tackle soaring fees?

Apart from regulating and reining in extreme fees, Grattan says the government could expand public clinics in areas with too little care, train more specialists, and give every GP easy access to specialist advice.

Grattan also wants to introduce an "annual rule" — where if a specialist's fees average more than triple the Medicare Benefits Schedule fee across a year, they would be required to pay back the Medicare rebates for their services that year.

This would affect fewer than 2,000 specialists — about 6 per cent.

"To make sure Australians can get the care they need, governments must fix those structural problems, not just spend more," it said.

title: Major Australian employers are cutting jobs. What does it mean for the economy?
text:
In brief Australia's biggest employers have cut thousands of jobs in recent weeks.

Some predict this could impact the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision on interest rates.

Some of Australia's biggest employers are cutting thousands of jobs, and economists are asking whether the "resilient" job market is starting to crack — and is another sign of an impending recession.

From banking and mining to digital services — the job cuts have been mixed across various sectors.

Last week, the country's digital design giant, Canva, announced it will cut or relocate more than 1,200 jobs — 22 per cent of its workforce — in what was described as the company's first restructuring in 13 years.

Just a day later, gas giant Woodside Energy announced it would cut at least 500 jobs globally as part of a cost-cutting process, with 80 per cent of its workforce based in Australia.

On the same day, the country's iconic retailer David Jones announced it had entered voluntary administration.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The job-cutting trend has also hit the banking sector, with National Australia Bank (NAB) announcing plans to cut 2,500 jobs by the end of the financial year in October.

"They're significant. In some cases, some of these businesses are shedding," Robert Breunig, an Australian National University pubic policy economist, told SBS News.

"It's hundreds or even thousands of jobs, and it's a large fraction of their workforce.

"But in terms of the number of overall jobs in the economy, it's still just a relatively small piece of the picture."

What's leading the major job cuts?

These under-pressure employers face different disruptions.

Canva co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said in a statement on the job cuts that "new technology is transforming what people can create" and "small changes won't be enough" — without directly naming artificial intelligence (AI).

David Jones's announcement came after years of mounting pressure on traditional department stores from changing shopping habits, online competition and expensive property decisions.

And NAB blamed challenging economic conditions, technological change, competition and a need to simplify its operating model.

Robert Brooks, a professor in the department of econometrics at Monash University, says each company announcement offers "different lessons" to be learnt.

"Canva is obviously a newer company at a much earlier stage, and it's working through what its appropriate business model is in a digital transformation setting," he told SBS News.

"David Jones is a mature company in a mature industry that's been significantly impacted by technological change and changing people's retail purchase patterns.

"The banking sector ones are somewhere in between. [They] are obviously a very mature and sophisticated economic sector. They're clearly in a business model that is being disrupted, but a lot of their business has a tremendous go-forward version."

A 'less resilient' job market

The job cuts have happened while Australia's unemployment rate climbed to 4.7 per cent in September — its highest level since October 2021, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

That figure, coupled with the company cuts, has raised questions about the strength of the job market.

"The [job] market has been really resilient up to a point. It's been able to absorb a lot of significant policy change, and it's been able to absorb a lot of geopolitical shocks," Brooks said.

"What we've seen in the more recent data is this picture where the market has become slightly less resilient.

He said although people should watch the current job market "incredibly carefully", there is not enough information to show that it has started to crack.

The ABS figure showed almost 40,000 people lost their jobs in September, while 732,000 people were unemployed nationwide.

Breunig said while Australia's job market is not doing as well as a year ago, the Australian economy remains pretty robust.

"We often talk about job losses because those are the things that get the media attention, but there are also thousands of jobs that are created every day. And Australia does have a very dynamic small business sector."

He warned that the rise in the unemployment rate might affect the country's economy as a whole.

"It does put the government in a difficult position because they're gonna have to pay more in income support payments to people. They're also gonna get less tax revenue from fewer workers," he said.

Is Australia headed for a recession?

More job losses are expected in the coming months following the Reserve Bank's rate hike in November from 4.6 per cent to 4.85 per cent — the highest since 2008.

Economists and social services groups are bracing for the unemployment rate to rise in the coming months, with higher interest rates generally leading to higher unemployment rates.

"The effect is that it makes people feel poorer because they're spending more money on their mortgage. So they have less money to spend in the economy ... and that ripples through to lower employment," Breunig said.

"And then, [in] the long term, AI is very likely to displace jobs. It will create other jobs, and other jobs will come along. But again, the kind of short- to medium-term effect of AI is also likely to push the unemployment rate up."

Persistently higher unemployment can affect the entire country's economy, potentially leading to a recession — something the RBA has said it wants to avoid.

One way of detecting the onset of a recession by measuring unemployment is the 'Sahm rule': it considers a recession is underway when the three-month average unemployment rate is at least 0.5 per cent higher than its lowest level in the past year. However, the RBA adjusts this to 0.75 per cent for Australia.

Here, the jobless rate averaged 4.63 per cent from July to September, up from 4.17 per cent between December and February — a 0.46-percentage-point increase that falls short of the Sahm rule threshold.

Last week, while announcing the fifth rate rise of the year, RBA governor Michele Bullock said that it will "make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer".

But she said the bank "is not looking to tip the economy into a recession if we can avoid it".

One factor that could influence a rate cut is rising unemployment.

The potential impact on employment was also among the factors the RBA's board considered at its last meeting, when six board members voted to raise rates, while three voted to leave them unchanged.

Brooks said part of the reason for the split vote was questions about whether the rate increase will have "a large spike in unemployment that the labour market can't quite deal with".

"I think from part of the commentary and the discussion that's come out from the recent decision, they are clearly going to need to take a look.

"More data that tells us that unemployment is continuing to rise would suggest that we wouldn't wanna push too hard further on contractionary monetary policy."

title: Donald Trump offers UFC chief Dana White job as White House press secretary
text:
In brief Donald Trump invited UFC chief Dana White to be the new White House press secretary in a social media post.

The White House press secretary role has been vacant since Katie Zacharia's brief tenure ended last month.

United States President Donald Trump has asked mixed martial arts promoter Dana White to serve as White House press secretary and called on him to bring some fighters along as assistants "even though some are not from our country."

White, chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, is a "violent fighter and warrior", Trump said in a Truth Social post on Sunday.

Trump also asked for six current or former UFC titleholders to join White, including two athletes from Russia's Dagestan region, Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov, Americans Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier and "Kayla Harris," likely a reference to Kayla Harrison, and Amanda Nunes, a Brazilian native who became a US citizen last year.

"We need these people to defend us against the lunatic left," Trump wrote.

White and UFC's parent company, TKO Group Holdings, did not immediately return requests for comment. However, CNN reported White has declined the presidentsy's invitation.

title: How thousands of 'special votes' will now determine New Zealand's election winner
text:
IN BRIEF The NZ election has ended without a clear winner.

The result could be decided by 700,000 votes and minor party negotiations.

It could be weeks before the winner of New Zealand's general election emerges, with neither of the two major parties securing enough seats to form a government.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party secured 42 seats in the country's parliament, while former Prime Minister Chris Hipkins' centre-left Labour Party won 36 seats.

The National Party, combined with its coalition partners ACT and NZ First, had a projected count of 67 seats, according to the NZ Electoral Commission.

Opposition parties Labour, the Greens and the Māori Party, together with the new force Opportunity — which has not yet said which side it will join in a coalition — combined for 63 seats.

Luxton has said that he is confident in securing another term, while Hipkins has said he will wait for the final results.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Final results in weeks

To control the New Zealand parliament, a party needs a majority of 61 seats out of the baseline 120 seats.

However, under New Zealand's Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) voting system, the total number of seats can increase because of "overhang seats", changing the number needed for a majority. Voters can decide how many seats a party gets during the election.

In the current election, the majority needed to lead is 66 seats, according to the country's public broadcaster, Radio New Zealand (RNZ).

READ MORE New Zealand election still on a knife edge with more than 90 per cent of votes counted

In the party vote, Labour had a narrow majority, with 29.36 per cent, while National secured 29.21 per cent, according to RNZ.

The Greens recorded their best-ever national vote, on 13.30 per cent, as did ACT, on 10.92 per cent, while NZ First was at 9.78 per cent and Opportunity at 5.96 per cent.

The results might also change when an estimated 700,000 'special votes' from out-of-electorate and overseas ballots — which typically favour the left — are added to the mix.

They will all be included on November 27, when the final results are released, meaning it might take weeks to understand who will be in charge of New Zealand's next government.

About 400,000 special votes remain to be counted, including 96,000 from overseas.

While the final results will be announced in weeks, the current New Zealand prime minister has said he is confident of a second term.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he's confident of another term in government while Labour leader Chris Hipkins says results are still being counted. Source: Getty, AAP / Hagen Hopkins / Ben McKay

'Time to sit tight'

Luxon said his National Party had secured the most seats, giving them a mandate to form government.

"Ultimately, New Zealanders have given us the biggest seats in parliament, 42 seats as it stands today and a pathway to form a government."

But he said his party and all New Zealanders now needed to wait for the final results on 27 November.

If he does secure another term, it could be without important figures in the election: finance minister Nicola Willis, defence minister Paul Goldsmith and speaker Gerry Brownlee, who all conceded their races, while transport minister Chris Bishop is also a likely loser.

"Some of the hardest phone calls tonight have been to colleagues and friends who look unlikely to make it back into parliament," Luxon said.

Meanwhile, Labour leader Chris Hipkins said on Saturday that he will wait for the final results.

"As things stand tonight, it's clear we're not going to know the exact shape of the next government for a little while longer yet," he said.

"When the final result is known, I'll have quite a bit more to say."

The results have followed weeks of election campaigns dominated by cost of living issues and the economy, with the country's unemployment rate at its highest in a decade.

The war in the Middle East and the resulting global fuel shock have been widely blamed for the damage to New Zealand's trade-dependent economy.

The outsider who could decide next government

Support for Labour and National has fallen to historically low levels. Surveys suggest voters have lost faith in the major parties' ability to revive the sluggish economy and make the changes needed to repair ageing infrastructure.

If the National-led coalition loses its majority at the official count, either it or a left-leaning coalition would require the support of the centrist Opportunity Party, which looks likely to enter parliament for the first time.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said she would seek to negotiate with the party that secured the most seats after the official results.

Wong has said she would look to negotiate with the party that secures the most seats in parliament and that it would be possible to find common ground with National or Labour.

Qiulae Wong has been a politician for less than a year, but the 38-year-old could hold the balance of power in New Zealand's parliament. Source: AP / Jonathan Killick / Stuff

Wong, a former sustainable-business consultant, answered an advertisement for the role of head of the decade-old party and took over in November 2025.

She quickly oversaw a rebrand and a dramatic rise in Opportunity's popularity.

The party's flagship policies centre on tax: An annual NZ$19,400 ($15,685) universal basic income for most New Zealand residents funded by a 1.75 per cent annual land tax. The party also wants to simplify the country's income tax system.

National and Labour have both ruled out adopting Opportunity's tax policies.

"It might seem like we've just arrived, that this is an overnight success, but to many in this room, this result has been a long time coming," Wong told cheering supporters in Auckland on Saturday night.

The fall in greenhouse gas emissions is linked to both the rapid deployment of renewable technologies and a fall in demand caused by oil prices shocks stemming from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which caused emissions from oil to fall 1.9 per cent. The Global Carbon Project, a collaboration of scientists tracking and analysing greenhouse pollution, found the dip in pollution it detected was not enough to signal a sustained declined.
